description: A plain-spoken breakdown of what a new manufactured home on land costs in Horry County, SC — the package model, what's bundled in, and why it beats buying the pieces separately.
bodyMarkdown:
If you've started pricing out a new home around the Grand Strand, you've probably run into the same confusing wall everyone does. One website quotes you a home price. Another quotes you land. Somebody else mentions delivery, and a fourth person starts talking about septic and power hookups. By the time you add it all up in your head, you have no idea what the real number is — or whether you can afford it.

Here's the honest version of how it works, and why buying a new home and the land it sits on as one package is usually the cleaner, cheaper way to do it here in Horry County.

## The "package" model, in plain English

When we talk about a land-home package, we mean exactly that: a brand-new manufactured home from a builder like Clayton, Cavco, or Champion, set on a piece of land you own, ready to live in. One deal. One closing. One number.

A typical package around Conway, Loris, Longs, Aynor, or the outskirts of Myrtle Beach includes:

- **The home itself** — new construction, your floor plan, your finishes.
- **A lot** — often around a quarter-acre, give or take, with no HOA telling you what color to paint the shutters.
- **Delivery and set** — getting the home to the site and properly installed and anchored.
- **Utilities and site work** — the well or water tap, septic or sewer connection, power, and the pad the home sits on.

That last bullet is the one people forget, and it's the one that wrecks budgets when folks try to buy the pieces separately. A home price by itself is not a move-in price. The package price gets you to move-in.

## So what does it actually cost?

Most new land-home packages in our area start in the **low $200s** and move up from there depending on the home's size, the floor plan, and the specific lot. A bigger home, a nicer kitchen, or a more desirable piece of land moves the number up. A smaller, efficient plan on a standard lot keeps it down.

We're not going to throw a fake "starting at" price at you to get you in the door and then surprise you later. Land cost moves with location and lot size. Site work moves with what the ground needs — some lots are ready to go, others need more grading or a longer utility run. The fastest way to get a real number for a real home on a real lot is to call us at **(843) 849-HOME** and we'll walk it with you.

What we *can* tell you plainly: the price you should care about is the all-in, on-the-land, ready-to-live-in number — not the sticker on the home alone. Always ask anyone you talk to whether their quote includes the land and the site work, because a lot of quotes out there don't.

## Why bundling beats buying the pieces separately

You *can* buy a home from one place, find land on your own, and hire out the delivery, the well, the septic, and the electrical separately. People do it. But it's usually slower, more stressful, and more expensive. Here's why the package wins:

- **No coordination headaches.** Buying separately means you're the general contractor whether you want to be or not. You're chasing the land seller, the home dealer, the well company, the septic installer, and the power company — and if one of them is late, everybody waits. In a package, that coordination is our job, not yours.
- **Fewer surprise costs.** When the pieces are quoted separately, the gaps between them are where budgets blow up. Who's paying for the culvert? The permit? The final grading? In a package, those line items live in one quote, so there's nothing hiding in the cracks.
- **One financing path.** This is the big one. Trying to finance raw land, a home, and improvements as three separate transactions is a paperwork nightmare. As a package, a new home on land can often be financed as a single home loan — and these typically qualify for **FHA, VA, or conventional financing** rather than the higher-rate, shorter-term loans people associate with older mobile homes.
- **It appraises and holds value like a home.** A new, permanently-set home on land you own is real property — not a vehicle title in a rented park. That matters for your loan, your taxes, and your resale down the road.

## What you own at the end — and the warranty

When the dust settles, you own the home *and* the land underneath it. No lot rent. No HOA. No landlord deciding to sell the park out from under you. For a lot of first-time buyers around here, that's the whole point — a real foundation, on real ground, with payments that often land near or below what they were paying to rent.

And because these are brand-new homes, they come with a **one-year warranty**. If something's off in that first year, it gets handled. That's a very different experience from buying a used home as-is and hoping for the best.

## A realistic way to think about your budget

If you're trying to ballpark this before you call, a sensible approach is:

1. Start with the low $200s as a floor for a new package in our area.
2. Add for size and floor plan — more square footage and more bedrooms cost more.
3. Add for the land — a larger or more in-demand lot costs more than a standard quarter-acre out toward Loris or Aynor.
4. Factor your financing — your rate, your down payment, and your loan type (FHA, VA, conventional) shape the monthly payment as much as the price does.

Then, instead of guessing, get a real quote on a real home and lot. That's the only number that actually matters.

title: FHA vs VA vs Conventional: Financing a Manufactured Home in SC
description: FHA, VA, and conventional loans for a manufactured home on land in Horry County, SC — down payments, who each fits, and how Home Placer connects you to lenders.
bodyMarkdown:
One of the first questions we hear from folks here in Horry County is some version of: "Can I actually get a real mortgage on a new manufactured home?" The short answer is yes. When you buy a brand-new Clayton, Cavco, or Champion home placed on land — titled as real property, the way we do it — you have the same main financing roads open to you as someone buying a stick-built house: FHA, VA, and conventional. The trick is knowing which road fits your situation.

We're not a lender, and we won't pretend to be. What we do is help you understand your options in plain English, then connect you with lenders who finance manufactured-home-on-land packages every day. Below is the honest rundown we'd give a neighbor.

## Why "home on land" changes everything

Before we compare loans, here's the piece that matters most. A manufactured home parked in a rental community on a leased lot is usually financed with a chattel (personal property) loan — shorter terms, higher rates. That is *not* what Home Placer sells.

We pair a new home **with the land** as one package, and the home is permanently set and titled as real property. That distinction is what unlocks FHA, VA, and conventional mortgages with the longer terms and friendlier rates you'd want. So as you read on, know that everything here assumes the land-and-home setup we specialize in across Conway, Loris, Longs, Aynor, and the wider Grand Strand.

## FHA loans: the first-timer's friend

FHA loans are backed by the Federal Housing Administration, and they're often the easiest door to walk through — especially for first-time and budget-conscious buyers.

- **Down payment:** as low as 3.5% with a qualifying credit score.
- **Credit:** more forgiving than conventional. Lower scores can still work, sometimes with a slightly larger down payment.
- **Best for:** first-time buyers, anyone who's rebuilding credit, or folks who simply don't have a big pile of cash saved.

The trade-off is mortgage insurance. FHA loans carry an upfront and an ongoing mortgage insurance premium, which adds to your monthly payment and typically stays for the life of the loan. For a lot of our buyers, that's a fair price to pay for getting into a brand-new home now instead of renting for three more years. FHA also has specific requirements for how the home is installed and foundationed — the good news is that the way Home Placer sets homes is built to meet them.

## VA loans: earned, and hard to beat

If you've served, this is the benefit you earned, and it's genuinely one of the best deals in housing. We've got a lot of military and veteran families along the Grand Strand, and we love helping them use this.

- **Down payment:** $0 down for eligible veterans, active-duty service members, and many surviving spouses.
- **Mortgage insurance:** none. That's a real monthly savings versus FHA.
- **Best for:** anyone with VA eligibility — full stop. If you qualify, this almost always beats the alternatives.

There is a one-time VA funding fee (some disabled veterans are exempt), and the home and land have to meet VA's standards. VA financing of a manufactured home is absolutely doable when it's set as real property on its own land, which is exactly our model. If you've got a Certificate of Eligibility or think you might qualify, tell us early so we point you to a VA-savvy lender.

## Conventional loans: when your file is strong

Conventional loans aren't government-backed; they follow Fannie Mae / Freddie Mac guidelines. They reward buyers with solid credit and a bit more to put down.

- **Down payment:** commonly 5% and up; programs exist as low as 3% for some buyers.
- **Mortgage insurance:** required if you put down less than 20%, **but** it can drop off once you've built enough equity — unlike FHA's. That long-term savings is the big draw.
- **Best for:** buyers with good-to-strong credit who want to ditch mortgage insurance down the road, or who are putting more money down.

Fannie Mae's MH Advantage and Freddie Mac's CHOICEHome programs specifically support qualifying manufactured homes with terms that look a lot like a regular mortgage. Not every home or buyer fits, but when it works, conventional can be the lowest long-run cost of the three.

## A quick side-by-side

- **Lowest down payment:** VA (often $0), then FHA (3.5%), then conventional (3–5%).
- **Easiest credit:** FHA, then VA, then conventional.
- **No mortgage insurance:** VA wins; conventional can shed it later; FHA generally keeps it.
- **Who it fits:** VA for those who served; FHA for first-timers and thinner credit; conventional for stronger files chasing long-term savings.

There's no universal "best." The right loan depends on your credit, your cash, your eligibility, and your goals. A good lender runs the numbers three ways and shows you the real monthly figure.

## We help every credit situation

Here's our promise: we don't write anybody off. Bruised credit, self-employed and hard to document, first time you've ever applied for anything — bring it. We've walked plenty of Carolina families from "I don't think we can" to keys in hand. Sometimes the answer is FHA today. Sometimes it's a few months of simple credit cleanup, then a stronger loan and a better rate. Either way, you'll get a straight answer.

Because we're not the lender, there's no pressure to steer you toward one product. We connect you with trusted lenders who know manufactured-home-on-land loans, and we sit on *your* side of the table while you compare offers.

## What it might cost — and the next step

Our new homes start in the low $200s with land included, no HOA, and a one-year warranty. What that turns into as a monthly payment depends entirely on your loan type, down payment, rate, and the specific home and lot. We won't quote you a number we can't stand behind — call for your exact figure and we'll get you real math, not a guess.

Walk into a Dutch Elite and you notice it immediately.

If a home that feels open and substantial matters to you, put Champion on your list — especially the Dutch Elite if those ceilings catch your eye.

title: Manufactured vs Modular vs Mobile: What is the Difference?
description: Manufactured, modular, and mobile homes are not the same thing. Here is a plain-English guide to HUD code vs modular code and what today's homes are really like.
bodyMarkdown:
If you have spent any time shopping for an affordable home around the Grand Strand, you have probably heard three words tossed around like they all mean the same thing: manufactured, modular, and mobile. They do not mean the same thing. The differences matter for how the home is built, how it is financed, what it is worth down the road, and even what you are allowed to put on your land.

We talk to first-time buyers in Conway, Loris, Longs, and Aynor every week who are surprised by what they learn. So let's clear it up in plain English, bust a few myths, and help you walk into your home search knowing exactly what you are looking at.

## The short version

Here is the whole thing in three sentences:

- A **mobile home** is an older home built before June 15, 1976. Technically, no one builds "mobile homes" anymore.
- A **manufactured home** is a home built in a factory after that date, to a national federal standard called the HUD Code.
- A **modular home** is also factory-built, but it follows your local or state building code instead of the HUD Code, and it is treated more like a traditional site-built house.

Everything else is detail. But the details are where buyers either save money or get tripped up, so let's go deeper.

## Why "mobile home" is an outdated term

The phrase "mobile home" sticks around because it is what people grew up saying. But it points to a specific era of housing. Before 1976, factory-built homes were genuinely a mixed bag. There was no single national standard, quality varied wildly, and the name "mobile home" fit because many were truly meant to be towed around.

That changed in 1976, when the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rolled out a federal construction and safety standard. From that day forward, every factory home built to that standard is officially a **manufactured home**, not a mobile home. The word "mobile" was retired on purpose.

So when someone calls a brand-new Clayton or Champion home a "mobile home," they are using a word that is nearly 50 years out of date. It is a little like calling a modern smartphone a car phone. The name carries baggage that simply does not match the product anymore.

## What the HUD Code actually means

The HUD Code is a real, enforced set of federal rules. Every manufactured home built today must meet it, and that is a big deal for you as a buyer. The code governs:

- **Structural design and strength** — how the home holds up under wind and load
- **Fire safety** — smoke detectors, escape windows, fire-resistant materials
- **Energy efficiency** — insulation and HVAC standards
- **Plumbing, heating, and electrical systems** — all inspected against one national benchmark

Because the standard is federal, a manufactured home built in a factory in one state meets the same baseline rules as one built anywhere else. Here in coastal South Carolina, homes are also built to the right **wind zone** for our area, which matters a lot when you live an hour from the Atlantic. Every HUD-code home gets a red certification label on the exterior proving it passed.

## How modular homes are different

Modular homes confuse people because they are also built in a factory, in sections, and trucked to the site. The difference is the rulebook. A modular home does **not** follow the HUD Code. Instead, it is built to the same state and local building codes as a house framed on-site, board by board.

Once a modular home is set on its foundation, it is generally treated like any other stick-built house for permitting, appraisal, and resale purposes. Modular homes often allow more design flexibility and multi-story layouts. The trade-off is usually cost: modular tends to run higher than manufactured, which is part of why manufactured homes remain the most affordable path to brand-new ownership.

Neither is "better." They are different tools for different budgets and lots. The right answer depends on your land, your loan, and your price target.

## Busting the myths

Let's knock down the tired ideas, because today's manufactured homes are nothing like the stereotypes.

- **Myth: They are flimsy.** Modern manufactured homes are built to a federal safety code, in a climate-controlled factory where materials never sit in the rain. Many buyers are shocked at how solid they feel.
- **Myth: They look cheap inside.** Walk through a new Clayton, Cavco, or Champion home and you will find drywall, real kitchen islands, walk-in pantries, soaking tubs, and finishes that look like any new build.
- **Myth: You can't get a real mortgage.** You can. Today's manufactured homes qualify for FHA, VA, and conventional financing, especially when the home is paired with land you own.
- **Myth: They don't hold value.** When a manufactured home sits on land you own and is properly placed and titled, it builds equity much more like a traditional home than the old rental-lot stereotype suggests.

## What this means for you here in Horry County

At Home Placer, we pair brand-new manufactured homes from Clayton, Cavco, and Champion **with land** as one package. That land piece is the part a lot of buyers miss. A home placed on a lot you own, with no HOA, financed with a real mortgage, behaves like the asset you actually want, not a depreciating box on a rented pad.

Our homes start in the low $200s, come with a one-year warranty, and qualify for FHA, VA, and conventional loans. We will not quote you a one-size-fits-all number, because your price depends on the home you choose and the land it sits on. For your exact number, just call.

Now you know the vocabulary: mobile is the old term, manufactured means HUD-code factory-built, and modular means factory-built to local code. Knowing the difference puts you in control of the conversation.

Ready to see what a new manufactured home and land package looks like for your budget? Call us at (843) 849-HOME and we will walk you through your options, no pressure.

title: Buying Land for Your Manufactured Home on the Grand Strand
description: A plain-spoken guide to buying land for a manufactured home in Horry County, SC — zoning, utilities, perc tests, access, and how Home Placer handles permits and setup.
bodyMarkdown:
A brand-new manufactured home is only half the story. The other half is the ground it sits on. Around the Grand Strand — Myrtle Beach, Conway, Loris, Longs, Aynor — the right lot can make your whole project smoother and cheaper, and the wrong lot can turn into a string of surprises. If you're thinking about putting a Clayton, Cavco, or Champion home on a piece of Carolina land, here's an honest look at what actually matters, and how we handle the parts most folks dread.

## What to Look For in a Lot

Not every pretty piece of land is a good piece of land to build on. Before you fall in love with a lot, walk through a short checklist.

**Zoning.** This is the first thing to confirm, every time. Horry County and the towns inside it each have their own rules about where a manufactured home is allowed and what size or type can go where. Some parcels are zoned for it outright. Others sit in areas with restrictions, or have old deed covenants that quietly limit what you can place. A lot that's perfect on paper does you no good if the county won't permit a home on it. The good news: we check zoning for you before anyone signs anything.

**Utilities.** Ask how the lot gets water, power, and sewer. Some Grand Strand lots tie into public water and sewer, which is the simplest path. Many rural parcels near Loris, Aynor, and Longs run on a private well and a septic system instead. Neither is wrong — but they change your timeline and your budget, so you want to know up front. Power is usually a matter of how far the nearest line runs and what the utility charges to bring service to your home site.

**Perc test and septic.** If there's no public sewer, the land needs a septic system, and that means a percolation ("perc") test. A soil evaluator checks how well the ground drains. Sandy, well-draining Carolina soil usually perks fine. Low, wet, or clay-heavy ground may need an engineered system, which costs more. This one matters because you can't skip it — a failed perc test can stop a project cold, so it's worth knowing the soil before you commit.

**Access and the home site itself.** Can a truck physically get the home onto the lot? A long, narrow, tree-lined drive or a soft, low spot can complicate delivery and setup. You also want enough cleared, level, buildable area for the home, the driveway, and the septic field — all on the same parcel, out of any flood-prone zone. A wooded acre sounds great until you price the clearing and grading.

None of this is meant to scare you off. Most lots around here work just fine. The point is to look before you leap, and to have someone in your corner who knows what they're looking at.

## Bring Your Own Land vs. One of Our Lots

There are two clean ways to do this, and we're glad to go either direction.

**Bring your own land.** Maybe it's been in the family. Maybe you already bought a parcel you love, or you found one for sale near where your people are. If you've got land, we'll put a home on it. We'll vet the lot first — zoning, utilities, perc, access — so we both know it's a buildable site, then handle the home, permits, and setup from there.

**Use one of our lots.** This is the easiest path for a lot of first-time buyers, and it's really what Home Placer is built around. We pair a brand-new manufactured home with land as one package — one price, one process, one team. The lots we offer have already been checked out, so you're not guessing about whether the ground will perk or whether the county will permit. Our packaged homes start in the low $200s with no HOA, and they qualify for FHA, VA, and conventional financing. Because the home and land come together, your lender sees one clean deal instead of two moving pieces, which usually makes financing simpler too.

There's no wrong choice between the two. If you already have land you're attached to, use it. If you'd rather skip the homework and move into a ready, vetted site, that's exactly what our packages are for. We'll lay out both options honestly and let you pick.

## How Home Placer Handles Permits and Setup

Once your lot is confirmed and your home is chosen, we manage the permitting through Horry County or the local town — the zoning and building permits, the septic permit and perc coordination if you're on septic, and the utility connections. We schedule delivery and the set: the home is placed on its foundation, leveled, blocked, anchored, and tied down to South Carolina's standards so it stands up to coastal weather. Then comes the button-up work — skirting, steps, utility hookups, and the inspections that sign off the home as ready to live in.

You don't need to become an expert in any of it. That's our job. And because these are brand-new homes, every one comes with a one-year warranty, so if something needs attention after move-in, you've got a number to call and a team that answers.

title: Do Manufactured Homes Hold Their Value? Myths vs Facts
description: Do manufactured homes lose value? The honest answer depends on land ownership and HUD-code quality. Here's the truth for Horry County buyers, myths and all.
bodyMarkdown:
If you've ever brought up manufactured homes at a family dinner, somebody probably said it: "Those things lose value the minute you move in, just like a car." It's one of the most repeated beliefs in real estate, and a lot of good people pass on a smart, affordable home because of it.

Here's the honest truth. That old saying isn't completely wrong, but it's nowhere near completely right either. Whether a manufactured home holds its value comes down to a few specific things, and most of them are in your control. Let's walk through it plainly, no sales pitch, just the facts as they actually shake out here in Horry County.

## Where the Depreciation Myth Comes From

The "manufactured homes always lose value" idea has real roots, and it's worth understanding so you can see why it doesn't apply the way people think.

Decades ago, older "mobile homes" were built with looser standards and were often sold by themselves, plopped into a rented lot in a park. When you own the home but rent the dirt underneath it, you own a structure with no land. And a structure with no land behaves a lot more like a vehicle than like real estate. It can be moved, it sits on someone else's property, and over time it can lose value the same way any building does when nobody's investing in the ground it sits on.

That's the scenario the myth is built on: an older home, on rented land, with no appreciating asset attached. Change those conditions, and the whole equation changes with it.

## The Real Driver of Value: Owning Your Land

Here's the part most people miss. In real estate, the land is usually what appreciates, not the building. A stick-built house in Conway from 1990 isn't worth more today because the lumber got fancier. It's worth more because the land under it, and the neighborhood around it, went up in value.

Manufactured homes work the exact same way. When you own the home AND the land it sits on, you own real property, the same legal category as any traditional house. Your home is permanently placed, titled with the land, and it appreciates or holds value based on the same forces that move every other property in the area: location, demand, and what's happening in the local market.

This is the whole reason Home Placer pairs a brand-new home with land as one package. You're not renting a lot. You're not buying a home that floats on someone else's property. You own the dirt, and the dirt is the part that grows.

The Grand Strand has been one of the steadier, more in-demand corners of South Carolina for years. People keep moving to Horry County. When you own land here and put a quality home on it, you're holding an asset in a place folks actually want to be.

## HUD-Code Quality Isn't What It Used to Be

The second half of the value story is the home itself, and this is where a lot of outdated thinking trips people up.

Every manufactured home built today is constructed to the federal HUD Code, a national building standard enforced since 1976 and toughened up several times since. That means today's homes from builders like Clayton, Cavco, and Champion are engineered for energy efficiency, wind resistance, fire safety, and structural strength. These aren't the thin-walled boxes your grandparents pictured.

A few things worth knowing:

- HUD-code homes are inspected at multiple stages during the build, in a controlled factory where weather never delays or damages the work.
- They're built to specific wind-zone ratings, which matters a great deal along the coast.
- Modern materials, insulation, and finishes mean the home looks, feels, and performs like any new construction.

A well-built home, kept up and cared for, holds up. When the structure is solid and the land underneath it is appreciating, you've got the two ingredients that actually drive long-term value.

## An Honest Look: What Still Affects Value

We promised balanced, so here it is straight. A few things genuinely do influence how a manufactured home holds value, and pretending otherwise wouldn't serve you:

- **Land ownership versus a rented lot.** This is the big one. Home on owned land equals real property. Home on rented land equals a much weaker value position. Choose owned land.
- **Maintenance.** Like any home, neglect costs you. A roof, skirting, and HVAC kept in good shape protect your number.
- **Location.** A home in a growing area holds value better than one in a declining one. Horry County's steady demand works in your favor here.
- **The local market.** Manufactured homes ride the same market waves as everything else. In a strong area, that's a tailwind.

Notice what's NOT on that list: the simple fact that it's a manufactured home. By itself, that doesn't doom your value. The conditions around it do the work, and most of those conditions are choices you get to make at the start.

## The Bottom Line for Carolina Buyers

So, do manufactured homes hold their value? When you own your land, buy a quality HUD-code home, and keep it up in a market people want to be in, yes, they can hold value right alongside traditional homes, and they let you get into ownership for a lot less to start, with homes from the low $200s.

bodyMarkdown:

## The Three Layers of Coverage

Your new home isn't protected by just one warranty. Three things work together, each doing a different job:

- **The full 1-year home warranty** — covers the home itself through your first year of ownership.

This is your first line of protection, and it's broad. For the first year you own the home, the home itself is under warranty. ## Demystifying the "2-10"

The term **2-10 Home Buyers Warranty** confuses a lot of people, so let's clear it up. The "2-10" isn't a brand gimmick — it's the name of a long-standing national new-home warranty program, and the numbers tell you exactly what you're getting:

There's an old assumption that a manufactured home is somehow flimsier or less "real" than a stick-built house. - **Report issues when you notice them.** Don't sit on a problem hoping it sorts itself out. The sooner you report, the easier it is to address — and the clearer it is that it's a covered defect rather than later wear.

- **When in doubt, ask.** You don't have to diagnose it yourself or figure out which warranty owns it. If something seems wrong, reach out and let the coverage do its job.

A new home from Home Placer is protected three ways at once: a **full 1-year warranty** on the home, a **2-10 Home Buyers Warranty** (two years on plumbing, electrical, and HVAC; ten years on the structure), and a **30-day walk-through** to catch the early stuff. title: Single-Wide vs. Double-Wide: How to Choose
description: A plain-spoken guide to single-wide, double-wide, and multi-section manufactured homes: space, layout, cost, land needs, and financing in Horry County, SC.
bodyMarkdown:
If you've started shopping for a manufactured home around the Grand Strand, you've probably run into the terms "single-wide" and "double-wide" before anyone explained what they actually mean for you. They sound like jargon, and the truth is the difference is pretty simple once you cut through it. It comes down to how wide the home is, how it gets to your land, and how much room and money you're working with.

Here's the honest rundown so you can walk into the decision knowing what each one really gives you, and what it asks of your lot and your budget.

## What the terms actually mean

A manufactured home is built in sections at a factory, then delivered to your land and set up on a permanent foundation. The "wide" part refers to how many sections the home comes in.

- **Single-wide** — one long, narrow section. It arrives in one piece and sits as one rectangle. These are the most compact, most affordable layouts.
- **Double-wide** — two sections that get joined together on-site, side by side, to make a much wider, more house-shaped footprint. This is what most people picture when they think "new manufactured home."
- **Triple-wide / multi-section** — three or more sections joined together for a wide-open footprint, bigger rooms, and floor plans that rival a site-built house. Less common, but a real option if you want the space and have the land for it.

All of these are HUD-code homes, built to a federal construction standard, and the ones we carry come from **Clayton, Cavco, and Champion**. Modern versions have drywall, real kitchens, energy-efficient construction, and floor plans that don't feel anything like the "trailers" people remember from decades ago.

## Space and layout: the real difference

This is where the choice gets practical. A single-wide is narrow, so the rooms tend to line up one after another and you walk through the home end to end. It's efficient and easy to keep up, and a well-designed single-wide can feel surprisingly open. If you want a comfortable home without a lot of extra rooms to clean and heat, it does the job.

A double-wide opens everything up. Because it's roughly twice as wide, you get:

- Wider living areas and an open kitchen-to-living flow
- Room for a larger primary suite, often with a walk-in closet and a bigger bath
- Hallways and bedrooms that feel like a standard house, not a corridor

A **triple-wide or multi-section** takes that even further: bigger great rooms, more bedrooms, sometimes a dedicated office or split bedroom layout. If square footage and an open feel are your priority, this is the top of the range.

A simple way to think about it: single-wides are great when you want simple and budget-friendly. Double-wides are the sweet spot for buyers who want a true house feel. Multi-section is for when you want maximum room and have the land and budget to match.

## What each one needs from your land

Here's the part people don't always think about up front. The wider the home, the more land you need to set it properly and meet setback rules, which are the required distances between your home and the property lines.

The good news: around here, **lots are often about a quarter-acre, give or take**, and that's plenty of room for a single- or double-wide in most cases. A multi-section home has a bigger footprint, so it wants a more generous lot, especially if you also want a yard, a driveway, and room for a porch or shed.

Because Home Placer sells the **home and the land as one package**, this is something we sort out for you. When you tell us which home you're drawn to, we make sure the lot actually fits it: setbacks, septic or sewer placement, the well or water line, power, and the driveway. You own the land outright, and there's **no HOA** telling you what you can and can't do with it.

## Cost: where the money goes

Let's keep this honest, because exact numbers depend on the home you pick, the land, and the site work. As a rule of thumb:

- **Single-wides** carry the lowest price because there's less home and a simpler set.
- **Double-wides** cost more than single-wides but give you a lot more home for the money, which is why they're the most popular choice.
- **Multi-section homes** sit at the top, with more material, more square footage, and a bigger set.

Our packages start **from the low $200s**, and that's the land plus a brand-new home, not just the box. Site costs like the foundation, utilities, and permits can vary depending on your specific lot, so the right move is to get a real quote rather than guess. We'll walk you through exactly what's included so there are no surprises.

## How financing fits in

A bigger home means a bigger loan, so the single-vs-double question and your financing question are tied together. **Home Placer isn't a lender** — we connect you with lenders who work with these homes — but here's the lay of the land:

- **USDA Rural Development** — $0 down for eligible rural areas, and much of Horry County qualifies, including the outskirts of Conway, Loris, Longs, and Aynor. Income limits apply and it has to be your primary residence.
- **VA loans** — $0 down for eligible veterans.
- **FHA** — as little as about 3.5% down, which keeps the upfront cost approachable.
- **Conventional** — a good fit for buyers with stronger credit.

The practical takeaway: if a double-wide is the home you really want but the monthly payment stretches you, a $0-down USDA or VA loan can make it work without a big down payment. A lender can tell you what you qualify for, and we're happy to point you to one.

## A quick word on peace of mind

Whichever size you choose, every new home we sell comes with a **full 1-year home warranty**, plus **2-10 warranty coverage** that runs about 2 years on systems like plumbing, electrical, and HVAC, and 10 years on major structural items. You also get a **30-day walk-through** after you move in, so anything you notice while settling in gets handled.

## So which one fits you?

Start with two questions: how much room do you actually need, and what land are you working with? If you want simple and affordable, a single-wide does more than you'd expect. If you want that true open-house feel, a double-wide is the sweet spot most buyers land on. And if you want maximum space, a multi-section is there for you.

The easiest way to figure it out is to talk it through with someone who can match a home to a real lot and a real budget. If you'd like a hand, give Home Placer a call at **(843) 849-HOME** or get in touch, and we'll help you weigh the options at your pace, no pressure either way.

title: Buying a Manufactured Home When Your Credit Isn't Perfect
description: Worried your credit will sink your home purchase? An honest look at the loan paths, what lenders actually weigh, and how to move forward.
bodyMarkdown:
Maybe you've been telling yourself for a while now that owning a home is off the table because of your credit. A late payment a few years back, some medical bills that went sideways, a number on a report that makes you wince. So you keep renting, and you keep wondering. Here's the honest truth: a credit score that isn't spotless does not automatically mean "no." It just means the path looks a little different, and the right lender matters more. Plenty of people buy a brand-new home on their own land in Horry County without a flawless financial history. Let's walk through how that actually works.

## Your Credit Score Is One Piece, Not the Whole Picture

It's easy to fixate on the three-digit number, but lenders look at a lot more than that. When they decide whether to approve a loan, they're trying to answer one basic question: can you reliably make the payments? Your score is part of that answer, but so are several other things.

Here's what typically goes into the decision:

- **Income and how steady it is.** A consistent paycheck or steady self-employment history carries real weight.
- **Debt-to-income ratio.** This is how much of your monthly income already goes toward debts. The more breathing room you have, the better.
- **Your recent payment history.** Lenders care a lot about what you've done lately. A recent stretch of on-time payments says more than something from years ago.
- **Down payment and savings.** Money in the bank, even a modest amount, signals stability.
- **The reason behind the rough patch.** A one-time hardship reads very differently than a long pattern.

So if your score isn't where you'd like it, take a breath. A strong, stable income and a clean recent track record can go a long way toward balancing out an imperfect past.

## The Loan Programs That Tend to Be More Forgiving

This is where a lot of folks are pleasantly surprised. There are loan programs built specifically to help people get into homes without requiring perfect credit or a huge pile of cash. Home Placer isn't a lender, but we connect you with lenders who work with these programs every day. Here are the main ones worth knowing about.

**FHA loans.** These are backed by the Federal Housing Administration and are often a good fit when your credit is still on the mend. FHA allows for a down payment as little as about 3.5% and tends to be more flexible on credit than conventional financing. For a lot of buyers, this is the doorway in.

**USDA Rural Development loans.** Much of Horry County qualifies as "rural" for USDA purposes, especially the areas around Conway, Loris, Longs, and the outskirts of Aynor. The big draw is $0 down for eligible buyers on a primary residence. There are income limits and the property has to be in an eligible area, but if you're buying out where the land is a little more open, this one is worth a serious look.

**VA loans.** If you're an eligible veteran, a VA loan offers $0 down and tends to be generous on terms. If you qualify, it's one of the strongest financing tools out there.

**Conventional loans.** If your credit is stronger, conventional financing may give you more options. And if you're not there yet, it can be a goal to work toward.

title: Owned Land vs. Leased Land: The One Choice That Decides Everything
description: Manufactured home on owned land vs leased land: why owning the lot means real property, real mortgages, appreciation, and no lot rent on the Grand Strand.
bodyMarkdown:
Almost every other question about buying a manufactured home — financing, brand, floor plan, where to put it — eventually traces back to one decision you make at the very start. The choice of a manufactured home on owned land vs leased land is the fork in the road that quietly decides everything that comes after it: whether your home gains value or loses it, what kind of loan you can get, and whether you're building equity or just paying rent on dirt you'll never own.

We'll lay it out straight, because this is the one thing we don't want anyone around the Grand Strand to get wrong.

## The two paths, side by side

When you buy a manufactured home, the home and the ground underneath it can be tied together two very different ways.

**Leased land (a land-lease park).** You buy or finance the home, but you rent the lot it sits on. You pay lot rent every month, often with yearly increases, and the park owner sets the rules. The home stays titled as personal property — basically a vehicle title, the same legal category as a car or a boat.

**Owned land.** You own the home and the land it sits on as one piece of real estate. The home is set on a permanent foundation, the old vehicle-style title is retired, and the whole thing becomes real property — the same legal category as any traditional house. No lot rent. No landlord. No park rules.

That second path is the only one we do at Home Placer. We've never put a family on leased land, and we never will. Once you see how the two compare, you'll understand why. You can see how the whole thing comes together on our [land packages page](/land-packages).

## Why a manufactured home on owned land vs leased land changes the money

The difference between these two paths is not a small thing. It reaches into the three areas that matter most for any home: value, financing, and your monthly cost.

**Value.** In real estate, the land is usually what appreciates, not the building. A home on a rented lot has no land attached to it, so it behaves more like the depreciating vehicle its title says it is. A home on land you own rides the same market as every other property nearby. Around here, that matters, because the Grand Strand stays in demand and people keep moving to [places like Conway, Loris, Longs, and Aynor](/locations).

**Financing.** This is where the gap gets wide. A home on leased land is usually financed with a chattel loan, which treats the home as personal property. Chattel loans tend to carry higher interest rates and shorter terms than a real mortgage. A home on owned land, set on a permanent foundation and titled as real property, can be financed with a real home loan — and that opens the door to FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional financing. Those are the same loan programs the buyer of any house would use. We break the whole picture down on our [financing page](/financing).

**Monthly cost.** Lot rent never builds you a thing. It's money out the door, every month, and it tends to climb over time. A mortgage payment on owned land builds equity, and for a lot of first-time buyers it can land near or even below what they were paying to rent.

## The financing piece, in plain terms

It's worth slowing down on financing, because it's the part people underestimate.

The government-backed loan programs — FHA, VA, and USDA — are built for real property. To use them on a manufactured home, the home generally has to be permanently affixed to a foundation and titled as real estate, not as personal property. A VA loan, for example, can only be secured by real property, and it typically requires a licensed engineer to certify the foundation. None of that is possible when the home sits on a rented lot with a vehicle title.

So the practical reality is this: choose leased land, and you've usually narrowed yourself down to higher-rate chattel financing. Choose owned land, and you keep the full menu of mortgage options open — the same ones everyone else gets. That single choice can mean a meaningfully different interest rate and a much longer loan term, which shows up in your payment every month for years.

## "But aren't these just mobile homes that lose value?"

This is the honest objection, so here's the honest answer.

The "they always lose value" reputation comes from a real situation: older homes, on rented lots, with no land attached. Strip the land out of any home and yes, what's left behaves more like a depreciating asset. That's the leased-land scenario in a nutshell.

But every manufactured home built today is constructed to the federal HUD Code, the national building standard in force since June 15, 1976 and strengthened several times since. Homes from builders like Clayton, Cavco, and Champion are engineered for energy efficiency, fire safety, and wind resistance. That last one is no small thing here. Horry and Georgetown counties sit in HUD Wind Zone II, the coastal tier with stricter wind standards, and today's homes are built to meet it.

Put a quality, HUD-code home on land you own, and you've assembled the two ingredients that actually drive long-term value: a solid structure and appreciating ground beneath it. The myth describes the leased-land path. It doesn't describe what we do. We get deeper into this in our piece on [whether manufactured homes hold their value](/blog/do-manufactured-homes-hold-value).

## What you actually own at the end

When the dust settles on an owned-land package, here's what you walk away with:

- **Real property, not a vehicle title.** The home and land are one piece of real estate.
- **A real mortgage.** FHA, VA, USDA, or conventional, instead of a higher-rate chattel loan.
- **No lot rent and no landlord.** Nobody can raise your rent or sell the park out from under you.
- **An asset that can appreciate.** Tied to land in a part of the state people keep moving to.
- **A brand-new home with a warranty.** Not a used box bought as-is.

You can see real examples of homes we've set on owned land across the Grand Strand on our [recently placed page](/recently-placed). Every one of them sits on ground the family owns. And if you're curious how a package actually comes together from first call to keys, our [process page](/process) walks through each step.

title: Personal Property vs. Real Property: Why a Permanent Foundation Changes Everything
description: Manufactured home real property vs personal property SC: how titling affects your rate, taxes, appraisal, insurance, and resale — in plain English.
bodyMarkdown:
One of the most confusing parts of buying a new manufactured home is something nobody warns you about up front: whether your home is legally treated as *personal property* or *real property*. It sounds like fine-print lawyer talk, but the manufactured home real property vs personal property SC question quietly decides your interest rate, your taxes, your insurance, and what your home is worth the day you sell. Let's walk through it the way we'd explain it to a neighbor at the kitchen table.

## Manufactured Home Real Property vs Personal Property SC: Two Ways to Title the Same Home

Here's the thing that trips people up: the exact same brand-new Clayton, Cavco, or Champion home can be either kind of property, depending on how it's set and titled.

When a manufactured home leaves the factory, South Carolina treats it like a vehicle. It gets a title through the **SC DMV** — the same office that titles your truck. That's **personal property**. The home rolls in on a chassis, sits on a rented or temporary setup, and on paper it's a movable thing you own, not a piece of the land.

The other path is to permanently affix that home to land you own, then **retire** the DMV title and convert the home to **real property**. At that point the home stops being a titled vehicle and legally becomes part of the dirt it sits on — the same legal category as any stick-built house in Conway or Loris.

Same home. Two completely different financial lives. That's the whole ballgame.

## How a Home Becomes Real Property in SC

In South Carolina, the bridge from personal property to real property is a recorded document — the **Manufactured Home Affidavit for the Retirement of Title Certificate**. Once it's filed with the Register of Deeds, state law says the home is treated as real property and the title is folded into the land's deed. People also call this "de-titling" or "retiring the title."

You can't do it on just any setup, though. To qualify, a few things have to be true:

- **You own the land** the home sits on. This is non-negotiable — you can't retire a title on rented or leased ground.
- The home is on a **permanent foundation** and properly affixed.
- The towing hitch, wheels, and axles are removed.
- Utilities are hooked up and the install meets local code.

That list is exactly how [Home Placer sets every home](/process). We don't park a home on a temporary stand and wish you luck — we place a brand-new home on land you own, on a permanent foundation, built to convert to real property from the start.

## Why It Changes Your Financing

This is the part that hits your wallet hardest. A home titled as personal property is usually financed with a **chattel loan** — shorter term, higher rate, the kind of loan you'd get on an RV or a car. That's where the old "manufactured homes are bad investments" reputation comes from.

Convert that same home to real property on land you own, and you unlock real mortgages: **FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional**. Longer terms, friendlier rates, the same loans your neighbor used on a site-built house. FHA, VA, and USDA all require the home to be set as real property on a permanent foundation — they won't touch a chattel deal. So the titling decision is also the door to the best financing on the board.

We're not a lender, but we connect you with the right ones and explain it all in plain English. If financing is your big question, our [financing page](/financing) lays out which loan fits which buyer.

## Taxes, Appraisal, Insurance, and Resale

Financing is the headline, but real property changes four more things:

- **Taxes.** South Carolina assesses an owner-occupied legal residence — including a manufactured home you own and live in on your own land — at the **4% assessment ratio**, the same favorable rate as any primary home. A home that isn't your owner-occupied legal residence, or that sits on a rented lot, generally falls into the higher **6%** ratio instead. Over the years you own the place, that gap adds up.
- **Appraisal.** As real property, your home is appraised against comparable homes and the land, by the same playbook used on every house in the neighborhood — not valued like a used vehicle on a depreciation schedule.
- **Insurance.** Real-property homes are typically insured with a standard **homeowner's policy** rather than the pricier, narrower coverage that often follows personal-property mobile homes.
- **Resale.** When you sell, a real-property home transfers by deed at closing like any house, and a buyer can use the same mortgages you did. A personal-property home tends to limit your buyer pool to cash and chattel financing — fewer buyers, weaker offers.

Put those together and you see why the manufactured home real property vs personal property SC distinction isn't paperwork trivia. It's the difference between owning a depreciating titled object and owning real estate that holds value alongside everything around it.

## The Honest Tradeoff

We promised straight talk, so here it is. Going the real-property route asks more of you up front. You need to **own land** (or buy it as part of your package), the home has to go on a permanent foundation, and the title retirement is a real step with real paperwork. A personal-property setup on a rented lot can look cheaper and faster on day one.

But that day-one shortcut is exactly what costs people for years — higher rate, a higher tax ratio, costlier insurance, and a home that's harder to resell. When you boil the manufactured home real property vs personal property SC choice down to dollars, owning the land and converting to real property flips every one of those. That's the entire reason we build our [land-and-home packages](/land-packages) the way we do, and why we walk every buyer through the difference between [buying new on owned land and going site-built](/manufactured-vs-site-built).

## Let's Figure Out Your Situation

If your head is spinning a little, that's normal — most buyers have never had anyone explain this part honestly. There's no quiz to pass and no pressure here. Take a look at our [available homes](/homes) to see what fits your budget, or just call us at **(843) 849-HOME** and we'll walk through your land, your loan options, and what real property would mean for your exact situation. You'll get a straight answer, not a sales pitch.

title: Will a Manufactured Home Survive a Hurricane? Wind Zones, Tie-Downs & SC Code
description: A new HUD-code manufactured home in hurricane Wind Zone 2 SC is built to a 100 mph coastal standard. What that means for storm safety on the Grand Strand.
bodyMarkdown:
If you're buying near the coast, the question comes up fast: will a manufactured home survive a hurricane? It's a fair worry, and the honest answer depends on two things most people never think to ask about — how the home is built, and how it's anchored to the ground. For any manufactured home, hurricane Wind Zone 2 SC building rules set by HUD govern both of those, and they make a real difference once you understand them.

Let's walk through it plainly — no scare tactics, no empty promises.

## First, "mobile home" and "manufactured home" are not the same thing

This trips up almost everyone, and it matters more here than just about anywhere.

Before June 15, 1976, factory-built homes were just called mobile homes. They were built to a patchwork of state, local, and voluntary rules, and the quality was all over the map. That's where most of the wind-damage footage you've seen on the news comes from — old homes, built before there was a real standard, often poorly anchored.

On June 15, 1976, that changed. HUD — the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development — put a single national construction and safety code in place. Everything built to that standard since is a **manufactured home**, not a mobile home. New Clayton, Cavco, and Champion homes are built to the current HUD Code, engineered, inspected, and stamped with a data plate that tells you exactly what the home was designed to handle.

So when someone pictures a "trailer" peeling apart in a storm, they're usually picturing something built before the code existed. That's not what we sell.

## What a manufactured home, hurricane Wind Zone 2 SC standards, and the data plate really mean

Here's the part that matters most on the Grand Strand.

HUD divides the country into wind zones, and the coast gets the stricter rules. South Carolina's nine coastal counties — **Beaufort, Berkeley, Charleston, Colleton, Dorchester, Georgetown, Horry, Jasper, and Williamsburg** — are all classified as Wind Zone II. If you're buying anywhere around Conway, Loris, Longs, Aynor, Myrtle Beach, Georgetown, or the rest of the Grand Strand, you're in Zone II.

What does that buy you? A home built for Wind Zone II has to be engineered to withstand **winds of about 100 mph**. Homes in the rest of the state, away from the coast, are built to a 70 mph standard. The coastal homes are anchored harder, framed tougher, and rated for more.

That doesn't make a home hurricane-proof — nothing on land is — but it does mean a new home placed here is built to a coastal standard on purpose, not by accident. The wind zone is printed right on the home's data plate, so it's verifiable, not a sales claim. You can browse the homes we place in this area on our [homes page](/homes), and every one set on the coast is built to that Zone II rating.

## The part that actually decides it: the anchoring

If there's one thing to take away from this whole article, it's this: **the most common reason a manufactured home takes wind damage isn't the home — it's bad installation.**

A new HUD-code home is only as strong as the system holding it to the earth, and that system is engineered, not optional. A properly installed home on the coast uses a network of steel ground anchors connected by metal straps to the home's steel frame. Done right, that ties the structure down against both the lift and the side-to-side push a storm throws at it.

This is exactly why buying new and having it set correctly beats inheriting an old home with mystery anchoring. When we place a home, the anchoring is part of the job — engineered to the site, permitted, and inspected. It's not a corner anybody gets to cut.

A few honest notes:

- **Carports, porches, and add-ons are the weak points.** They catch wind and can fail before the home does. They need their own reinforcement, and they should never be an afterthought.
- **Anchors need to stay healthy.** Years down the road, straps can loosen or rust. A quick look now and then keeps the system doing its job.
- **Proper installation is everything.** A great home set poorly is a bad outcome. A solid home set right is what you want — and what you should insist on.

## New, on land you own, titled as a house

There's a quieter advantage that comes with buying new and placing it on land you own. A home that's permanently affixed and titled as real property — not sitting on a rented lot with a vehicle-style title — is treated like a house. That's what lets these homes qualify for conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA financing, and it's the same reason your homeowner's insurance treats it as a real structure.

It also means the home was set to stay: permanent foundation, engineered anchoring, real utility hookups. You can read more about the builders we work with on our [brands page](/brands), and walk through how a placement actually comes together on our [process page](/process).

## What we can — and can't — promise

We're not going to tell you a home will shrug off a Category 4. Nobody honest will tell you that about any home, stick-built or manufactured. Hurricanes are hurricanes, and the right move in a serious storm is always to follow local evacuation guidance.

What we *can* tell you is straight: a new HUD-code manufactured home in hurricane Wind Zone 2 SC is engineered to a 100 mph coastal standard, anchored with an engineered steel system, and — because it's new — backed by a **one-year warranty** on the home itself. If you've found a lot you love around the Grand Strand — or you already own one — the first nervous question is almost always the same: can I actually put a home on it? It's a fair thing to worry about, and understanding the basics of **horry county manufactured home zoning regulations** is the difference between a smooth project and a stalled one. The good news is that the rules are knowable, the process is routine, and you don't have to figure it out alone.

Here's the honest, plain-English version of what governs whether a new manufactured home can sit on a given piece of land in Horry County — zoning, setbacks, septic, and utilities — and how we handle the parts that trip people up.

## First: not every lot is the same, and that's okay

People sometimes assume land is land — if you own it, you can build on it. In reality, every parcel in Horry County carries a zoning designation, and that designation decides what you're allowed to do there. Some districts welcome a single manufactured home on an individual lot. Others are written for site-built houses, or for denser development, or for agricultural use with different rules attached.

The county ties its residential zoning classifications to minimum lot size. What that means for you is simple: the same home that's perfectly fine on one parcel might not be permitted a mile down the road. This isn't a reason to panic — it's just the reason you check *before* you fall in love with a lot, not after. If you're still shopping for ground, our guide to [buying land for a manufactured home on the Grand Strand](/blog/buying-land-for-manufactured-home-grand-strand) walks through what to look for.

Every parcel has a tax map number, a ten-digit ID the county uses to look it up. With that number, Horry County Planning and Zoning can tell you exactly how a property is zoned and what's allowed on it. We pull that for any lot we're looking at with you, so we're never guessing.

## What horry county manufactured home zoning regulations actually require

When a manufactured home is allowed on a lot, the county still expects it to be done right. A couple of baseline points hold across the board:

- **It has to be a real, permanent installation.** The home goes on a permanent foundation, properly anchored and underpinned to HUD standards. This isn't a trailer you park — it's a home you affix to the ground to stay.
- **It has to respect the setbacks.** Every district has minimum distances the home must sit back from the front, sides, and rear of your property line. Those distances vary by zoning district, so a smaller lot in one classification leaves you a different buildable footprint than a larger lot in another.

Setbacks are the rule people underestimate most. They quietly shrink the usable area of a lot, and on a tight parcel they can dictate which floor plans actually fit and how the home gets oriented. It's rarely a dealbreaker — but it's exactly the kind of thing you want measured early, not discovered late.

## Septic and the SCDES permit you can't skip

If your lot isn't on public sewer — and plenty of land out toward Loris, Longs, Aynor, and the rural edges of Conway isn't — you'll need a septic system. In South Carolina, that's permitted by the state environmental agency (SCDES), and there's an order of operations that matters: **the county generally won't issue your building permit until the state has approved the septic.** So septic isn't a detail you handle later. It's a gate near the front of the line.

Before the state issues a septic permit, an evaluator comes out and reads the soil. They take borings, look at how the ground is built, and check how high the water table climbs in the wettest part of the year. That soil evaluation decides whether a standard system works, whether you need a larger or engineered system, or whether part of the lot simply won't drain well enough to support one. It's the single biggest unknown on a raw lot, which is why a real **site evaluation** is worth its weight in gold before you commit.

A few honest realities about septic here:

- **Wet ground slows everything.** If the soil is too saturated, the evaluation may have to wait until it dries out. The Grand Strand's flat, low-lying land makes this more common than people expect.
- **Not all lots perc the same.** Two parcels side by side can grade out differently. The only way to know yours is to test it.
- **The system has to fit the home.** A four-bedroom home needs more drainfield than a two-bedroom. Bedroom count, lot size, and soil all have to line up.

## Utilities: water and power still have to reach the home

Beyond septic, the home needs water and electricity. If there's a public water line at the road, you'll tap into it; if not, the lot needs a well. Power has to be run from the nearest connection to a properly placed meter and panel. On a lot that's already been built near, this is straightforward. On a deeper or more remote parcel, a longer utility run is real money — and it's another line item that's easy to forget when you're only looking at the price of the home.

None of this is exotic. It's the standard checklist for putting any home on rural or semi-rural land. It just adds up to more moving parts than most first-time buyers expect, and the parts have to happen in the right order. If you want a sense of how those steps stack up, our [manufactured home on land timeline for Horry County](/blog/manufactured-home-on-land-timeline-horry-county) lays out the sequence start to finish.

title: What It Really Costs to Insure a Manufactured Home in South Carolina

When folks here on the Grand Strand sit down to figure out what a new home will actually cost them each month, they think about the mortgage and forget the line item right next to it: insurance. On the coast, that line matters. The good news is that **manufactured home insurance cost in South Carolina** isn't one fixed number handed down from on high — it's driven by a handful of factors you have real control over, and buying a brand-new home on land you own tilts most of them in your favor.

We're not insurance agents, and we won't pretend to be. But we walk buyers through the total monthly picture every week, so here's the honest breakdown of what drives the cost, why it's different near the ocean, and how to keep it as low as it reasonably can be.

## What drives manufactured home insurance cost in South Carolina near the coast

Let's be straight about where we live. Horry and Georgetown counties sit in a coastal wind zone, which means insurers price for one thing above all else: storms. Wind and hail are the big drivers here, not the everyday risks you'd worry about inland.

A few things follow from that, and it helps to know them going in:

- **Wind and hail can be a separate piece of coverage.** In coastal South Carolina, many policies break wind and hail out on their own — sometimes through the state's wind and hail association if a standard carrier won't write it. That coverage usually carries its own deductible.
- **Wind deductibles are often a percentage, not a flat number.** Instead of a fixed dollar deductible, your storm deductible may be a percentage of your home's insured value. Understand that number before you sign, because it's what you'd pay out of pocket after a hurricane.
- **Flood is its own policy.** Flood is never part of a standard homeowner's policy — anywhere. If your lot is in or near a flood zone, you'll likely carry separate flood coverage. Where your home sits, and how high it sits, affects that.

None of this is meant to scare you off the coast. People insure homes here every single day. The point is simply that the number isn't random — it tracks the real risks of where you're building.

## Why a NEW real-property home insures better than an old mobile home

Here's the part most buyers never hear, and it's the heart of the whole thing. There is a world of difference between insuring a 1980s mobile home on a rented lot and insuring a brand-new Clayton, Cavco, or Champion home that's permanently set on land you own.

That difference shows up in two big ways.

**First, how it's built.** Every new home we place is built to the federal HUD Code, which has governed manufactured housing since 1976 — and our coastal counties fall under HUD's higher coastal wind-zone standard. In plain terms, new homes going onto land here are engineered and anchored to stand up to coastal winds in a way the old "trailers" never were. Insurers know the difference between a pre-1976 mobile home and a modern, properly anchored, HUD wind-zone home, and they price accordingly.

**Second, how it's titled.** This is the quiet game-changer. An older mobile home on a leased lot is usually titled as personal property — chattel, the same legal bucket as a vehicle. A home we place is permanently affixed to your land and titled as **real property**, just like a stick-built house. That single distinction is what lets you insure it as a true homeowner's policy rather than the pricier, narrower mobile-home coverage that gets attached to chattel.

It's the same move that opens up conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA financing — which we walk through in detail on our [financing page](/financing). New construction plus real-property titling doesn't just help you borrow better. It helps you insure better, too. The home is treated like what it actually is: a permanent house.

## What you can actually do to lower the cost

You're not powerless here. Several of the biggest factors behind manufactured home insurance cost in South Carolina are things you influence before you ever pick a floor plan.

- **Own the land and title the home as real property.** This is the foundation of everything above. It's how our buyers get standard homeowner's coverage instead of chattel-only mobile-home policies.
- **Build new to current wind standards.** A new HUD wind-zone home with a proper foundation and anchoring is a far better risk than a decades-old unit, and that tends to be reflected in what carriers will offer.
- **Pay attention to the lot, not just the home.** Two lots a few miles apart can carry very different flood and wind exposure. A higher, drier lot outside a high-risk flood zone is generally cheaper to insure. We can talk that through when you're choosing where to place.
- **Bundle and shop.** Many buyers save by bundling home and auto, and by getting more than one quote. The wind-and-hail piece in particular can vary between carriers, so it pays to compare.
- **Mind your deductibles.** A higher wind deductible usually lowers your premium — but make sure it's a number you could actually cover after a storm. That's a personal call, not a one-size answer.
- **Ask about wind-mitigation features.** Construction and tie-down details that resist wind can matter to carriers. Keep the paperwork from your installation; it documents how the home was built and set.

A good local agent who writes coastal policies every day is your best ally here. They'll know which carriers are comfortable with new manufactured homes on owned land in our area, and they'll build the wind, hail, and flood pieces to fit your specific lot.

When you're budgeting, think of your monthly cost as a stack: principal and interest, property taxes, and insurance — homeowner's plus, where it applies, wind/hail and flood. Insurance is a real part of that stack on the coast, and pretending otherwise just leads to a payment that surprises you later. We'd rather you see the whole number up front.

The encouraging news is that nearly everything that makes coastal insurance expensive is worst for old, untitled, poorly anchored homes. By buying new, owning your land, and titling as real property, you land on the better side of every one of those factors. It's the same reason these homes hold up structurally and stay protected — which is also why they come backed by a real [new-home warranty](/warranty) instead of an as-is shrug. New and permanent simply gets treated better, by lenders and insurers alike.

title: Do Manufactured Homes on Permanent Foundations Appreciate? An Honest Answer
description: Do manufactured homes on permanent foundations appreciate? An honest look at when they hold value like real estate — and when they don't.
bodyMarkdown:
"Manufactured homes are a bad investment — they go down in value like a car." You've heard it, and if you're the kind of buyer who runs the numbers before you sign anything, it's a fair thing to worry about. So let's deal with it head-on: **do manufactured homes on permanent foundations appreciate**, or are you buying a depreciating box?

The honest answer is "it depends," and what it depends on matters more than almost anything else in the deal. Some manufactured homes really do lose value. Others behave like any other house on the street. The difference isn't the home — it's how and where it sits.

## Where the "bad investment" reputation comes from

The reputation is earned, but it's earned by a specific kind of home, not all of them.

Two situations make a manufactured home behave like a depreciating asset:

- **It sits on rented land.** A home in a park where you pay lot rent isn't tied to a piece of real estate you own. You own the structure; somebody else owns the dirt. When you go to sell, the buyer is buying a thing that has to be financed like personal property — on shorter terms at higher rates — and that drags the price down.
- **It's old, or titled as personal property.** Homes built before the federal HUD Code took effect on **June 15, 1976** were built to a patchwork of weaker standards. And any home that still carries a vehicle-style title — wheels-and-axle, registered like a car — is treated as personal property, which historically depreciates the way a vehicle does.

That's the version of the manufactured home that earned the bad rap. If that's the only kind you've ever seen, the skepticism makes sense. But it's not the only kind, and it's not what we sell.

## Do manufactured homes on permanent foundations appreciate? Here's what the research says

Here's the part that surprises people. When a manufactured home is set on a **permanent foundation on land the owner owns** and titled as **real property**, it stops behaving like a vehicle and starts behaving like a house.

A multi-county study out of East Carolina University — published by the North Carolina Manufactured & Modular Homebuilders Association, in the state right next door to us — looked at exactly this question. Researchers compared property valuations across four counties and found that a manufactured home on a fixed foundation, listed as real property, **appreciated at rates comparable to site-built homes** in the same area. The homes that behaved differently were the ones titled as personal property, not the ones tied to the land.

That tracks with how appraisers look at it, too. Value follows classification:

- **Real property** — permanent foundation, owned land, deeded — tends to move with the local housing market, up or down, like any other home.
- **Personal property** — rented lot or vehicle title — tends to depreciate.

So the question "do manufactured homes on permanent foundations appreciate" isn't really about manufactured homes at all. It's about whether the home is real estate or not. Put it on a foundation, put it on your own land, retire the title, and you've changed the category it competes in. We dig deeper into this in our companion piece on whether [manufactured homes hold their value](/blog/do-manufactured-homes-hold-value).

## What "real property" actually means in South Carolina

This isn't a marketing word. South Carolina has an actual legal process for it.

Under state law (the title-retirement statute, **§ 56-19-510**), once a manufactured home is affixed to the land, the wheels, axles, and hitch are removed, and the owner records a **Manufactured Home Affidavit for the Retirement of Title Certificate** with the register of deeds, the home is **treated for all purposes as real property**. The affidavit gets recorded like a deed, and the county assessor is notified. From that point on, the home and the land are one piece of real estate in the eyes of the county and the tax office.

That's the legal switch that turns a "mobile home" into a house. It's the same switch that lenders look for.

## Why financing proves the point

If you want outside confirmation that a permanently-set home on owned land is treated like real estate, look at who's willing to lend on it.

A new manufactured home on a permanent foundation, titled as real property on land you own, can qualify for the same mortgages a stick-built house does — **FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional** loans. Every one of those programs requires basically the same thing: a permanent foundation, real-property classification, and that you own (or are buying) the land underneath it.

Lenders don't write 30-year, real-property mortgages on depreciating assets. The fact that these homes qualify for the same long-term, government-backed financing as any other house tells you how the market actually categorizes them. (If you want the breakdown of which loan fits which buyer, our [financing guide](/financing) walks through it.)

There's a build-quality piece, too. Coastal South Carolina — Horry and Georgetown counties included — sits in **HUD Wind Zone II**, so new homes delivered here are engineered for higher wind loads than homes built for inland zones. A new home built to today's HUD Code is a very different structure than the 1980s single-wide most people picture.

## The honest tradeoffs

We said we'd be straight, so here are the real caveats:

- **Appreciation isn't guaranteed.** Real property follows the local market, and markets can go down. A home on a foundation isn't a magic money machine — it just rises and falls with the neighborhood instead of dropping like a vehicle.
- **The land does a lot of the work.** A big part of what holds and grows value is the dirt. Owning your lot — no lot rent, no HOA, no landlord selling the park out from under you — is the foundation of the whole investment, literally and financially. It's the core of every [land-and-home package](/land-packages) we put together.
- **Condition and care still matter.** Like any house, a neglected one is worth less than a maintained one.

None of that is unique to manufactured homes. It's just how owning real estate works.

## This is a real, active market — not a theory

You don't have to take the appreciation argument on faith. There's an active local market for exactly this kind of home right now.

Over the past several months we've placed new homes on owned land across **Conway, Longs, Loris, and Aynor** — real lots, real buyers, recorded as real property. You can browse the actual homes we've recently set, with towns and sale prices, on our [recently placed](/recently-placed) page. We're not going to put made-up return percentages in front of you — but a steady stream of new homes closing as real estate is the clearest sign there is that buyers and lenders treat these as the real deal.

## The bottom line

A used home on a rented lot can absolutely be a bad investment. A brand-new home on a permanent foundation, on land you own, titled as real property, is a different animal — it appreciates or holds value the way the rest of the neighborhood does.

If you're weighing the numbers and want a straight answer for a specific home on a specific lot, that's exactly the conversation we have every day here in Horry County. Take a look at what we've [recently placed](/recently-placed), or call Home Placer at **(843) 849-HOME** and we'll walk through the real math with you — no hype, no pressure.

title: The Biggest Mistakes Buying a Manufactured Home (and How to Avoid Them)
