Buying a brand-new home is a big deal, and most folks researching it for the first time are nervous about making an expensive wrong turn. The good news: almost every one of the common mistakes buying a manufactured home comes down to a handful of decisions you can get right up front — if somebody just tells you straight what they are.

So here's the honest rundown of the biggest mistakes buying a manufactured home. Each one below is a real one we see people make around the Grand Strand, followed by the move that actually protects you.

## Mistake #1: Buying a home to put on land you don't own

This is the big one, and it's the root of half the other mistakes on this list. A lot of people buy a home and rent the dirt under it — a leased lot in a park or a "land-lease" community. The home is yours; the ground isn't.

The problem is you're building a payment on something you'll never own. The park can raise the lot rent. The park can sell. And when you go to leave, a home in a rented park is hard to sell and rarely worth what you paid.

**The fix:** buy the home and the land together, as one package. You own the dirt, there's no lot rent, and no landlord deciding to sell the park out from under you. That's the whole model we build around — a new home on land you own, titled as real property. You can see how the pieces fit on our [land-home packages](/land-packages) page.

## Mistake #2: Taking a chattel loan when you could get a mortgage

Here's a term worth knowing before you sign anything: **chattel loan**. A chattel loan is a loan against personal property — the home is financed more like a vehicle than a house. They're common in the manufactured world, and they're often the wrong tool.

Compared to a real mortgage, chattel loans generally carry higher interest rates, shorter terms, and fewer consumer protections. Over the life of the loan, that gap can cost you real money every single month.

**The fix:** when your new home is permanently set on land you own and titled as real property, it can usually be financed as a regular home loan — and these often qualify for FHA, VA, USDA, or conventional financing instead. Same buyer, same home, a very different monthly payment. We break down the loan types on our [financing](/financing) page.

## Mistake #3: Skipping the permanent foundation

Some buyers try to save a little up front by setting the home on a temporary or minimal setup. It feels like a smart cut. It isn't.

A permanent foundation isn't just about the home sitting solid. It's the thing that turns your home from "personal property" into **real property** in the eyes of the county and your lender. No permanent foundation, no real-property title — and without that, the better loans simply aren't available to you. FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional financing all require the home to be on a permanent foundation and taxed as real estate.

**The fix:** treat the permanent foundation as non-negotiable. In a package, it's already baked in — the home is set, anchored, and affixed properly so it qualifies as real property from day one.

## Mistake #4: Ignoring wind zone and setup quality on the coast

We live on the coast, and that matters more than people realize. Manufactured homes are built to a federal HUD standard, and that standard is tougher near the ocean. Horry and Georgetown counties sit in HUD Wind Zone II, which means a home placed here has to be built to withstand higher winds than a home going up inland.

Buy a home rated for the wrong zone — say, a unit built for an inland market — and the county won't approve the installation. The wind rating is printed on the home's data plate, and the permit office checks it.

**The fix:** make sure the home you're buying is actually rated and built for our area, and that it's set and anchored by people who do it here every day. This is exactly why local matters. A new home placed correctly for Zone II isn't a worry — it's the standard.

## Mistake #5: Having no real plan for the land and site work

A home price is not a move-in price. People see a sticker number on a home, fall in love, and forget the land underneath it has to be *ready* — graded, with a well or water tap, septic or sewer, power, and a proper pad. Skip that planning and the surprise costs pile up fast.

**The fix:** price the whole thing, not just the box. The number that matters is the all-in, on-the-land, ready-to-live-in figure. When it's a package, that site work lives in one quote instead of hiding in the gaps between five different contractors. Our [process](/process) page walks through how a placement actually goes, start to finish.

## Mistake #6: Buying a used home when new makes more sense

A used home can look like a bargain, and sometimes it is. But buying used often means inheriting someone else's wiring, someone else's roof, and no warranty when something goes wrong. Older units may also predate the modern HUD code entirely, which can limit your financing and your insurance.

**The fix:** at least price a new home before you commit to used. New construction means current code, modern efficiency, your floor plan, your finishes — and because it's brand-new, it comes with a one-year warranty. If something's off in that first year, it gets handled instead of becoming your problem. You can browse current floor plans on our [homes](/homes) page.

## One more thing people get wrong: "manufactured" and "mobile" aren't the same

Plenty of folks use "mobile home" out of habit, picture something from decades ago, and write off the whole category. Today's manufactured homes are built to a federal code, set permanently on land, and financed like any other house. If the old terminology is tripping you up, our plain-English [manufactured home vs. mobile home](/mobile-home-vs-manufactured-home) explainer clears it up in a couple of minutes.

## The short version: how to avoid the biggest mistakes buying a manufactured home

Most of these mistakes rhyme with each other: they come from treating the home like a temporary thing instead of a real one. Own the land. Get the real-property title. Put it on a permanent foundation. Match the wind zone. Plan the whole site. Then finance it like the house it actually is.

Get those right and you don't have a "mobile home" — you have a new home, on your own ground, with a payment that, depending on the home and your financing, can land near or below what you'd pay to rent.

title: Site Prep & Land Readiness: Getting Your Horry County Lot Ready for a New Home
description: Manufactured home site prep in Horry County: clearing, grading, fill, the pad, driveway and utility taps on sandy Grand Strand soil — and how we handle it.
bodyMarkdown:
You've picked the home, you've got the lot — and then someone mentions "site prep," and you realize there's a whole step between bare ground and a finished home you hadn't pictured. That's the part this post is about. Done right, **manufactured home site prep in Horry County** turns a raw piece of land into a stable, dry, permitted home site. Done wrong — or skipped — it causes problems for years.

Here's the honest, plain-English version of what site prep involves around the Grand Strand, why our sandy-over-clay soils make it matter, and how we handle the heavy parts so you don't have to become an expert in dirt.

## What "site prep" actually means

Site prep is everything that happens to your lot *before* the home shows up, so the home has somewhere solid and legal to sit. On a typical Horry County parcel that usually includes:

- **Clearing** — removing trees, brush, stumps, and roots from the footprint where the home, driveway, and utilities will go.
- **Grading** — shaping the ground so water runs *away* from the home, not toward it. On our flat, low-lying land, drainage is half the battle.
- **Fill and compaction** — bringing in and packing down soil where the ground is too low, too soft, or too wet to build on as-is.
- **The pad** — the prepared, compacted base the home's permanent foundation sits on.
- **Driveway** — a stable way to get a delivery truck in and you in and out year-round.
- **Utility taps** — running water (or a well), power, and septic (or sewer) to where the home will be.

None of it is exotic — it's the standard checklist for putting any home on rural or semi-rural land. There are just more moving parts than most first-time buyers expect, and they have to happen in the right order.

## Sandy vs. clay: why Grand Strand soil drives the work

This is where local matters. The Horry County coastal plain is mostly **sandy topsoil sitting over clay**, and the mix changes from one lot to the next — sometimes from one corner of a lot to the other. Each type brings a tradeoff:

- **Sandy soil drains well but has lower bearing capacity.** Water moves through it fast, which is good — but loose sand can shift and settle under weight if it isn't properly compacted.
- **Clay holds weight but holds water.** It can support a home, but it drains slowly and swells when it's wet, which is exactly what you don't want pushing on a foundation.

On top of that, the water table here often sits just a few feet down and climbs in the wet season. That's why grading and drainage aren't afterthoughts on the Grand Strand — they're the main event. The goal of good manufactured home site prep in Horry County is a pad that stays dry and doesn't move, whatever the soil is doing underneath it.

## Fill, compaction, and the pad

When a lot is too low or too soft, the fix is fill — but *how* it goes in is what counts. Fill dumped in one big load and left alone settles unevenly, and an uneven settle is what cracks things over time. Done right, fill goes in **lifts** — layers — and each layer gets compacted before the next goes on. That's slower and costs more, and it's the difference between a pad that holds for decades and one that doesn't.

The pad itself is the prepared base your home's permanent foundation ties into. Because we install these as real, permanently affixed homes — anchored and underpinned to HUD standards, not parked — the pad has to be right. Horry County sits in HUD Wind Zone II, so the home is tied down for coastal wind, and those anchors are only as good as the compacted ground they transfer load into. A permanent foundation is also what lets the home be titled as real property and financed like any other house, so this step quietly protects your money two ways: the home stays put, and it stays financeable and appraisable.

## The driveway and utility taps

Two pieces buyers almost always forget when they're only looking at the price of the home:

- **The driveway.** A factory-built home is delivered on a truck, and that truck has to reach the pad — including in our wet season, when an ungraded dirt path turns to soup. You'll also want to get in and out every day after. A proper, stable drive is part of the job, not an extra.
- **Utility runs.** Water, power, and waste all have to physically reach the home. If there's public water and power at the road, you tap in; if not, the lot may need a well, and most rural parcels out toward Loris, Longs, and Aynor need a **septic system**. Septic is permitted by the state (SCDES), and it starts with a soil evaluation — an evaluator reads the dirt and the water table to size the system. The deeper or more remote the lot, the longer the utility runs — real money.

We go deep on the permitting side in our companion post on [Horry County zoning, setbacks, and septic](/blog/horry-county-manufactured-home-zoning-setbacks-septic), and you can see where site prep falls in the overall sequence in our [pick-to-keys timeline](/blog/manufactured-home-on-land-timeline-horry-county).

title: Septic, Perc Tests & Wells: Your Septic System Manufactured Home Horry County Guide
description: Septic permit, perc/soil test and well basics for a septic system manufactured home Horry County buyers can finance on rural Grand Strand land.
bodyMarkdown:
You found a quiet lot out past Conway or Loris, the price made sense, and then somebody mentioned a word that stopped you cold: septic. If you're buying rural land out here, getting a **septic system manufactured home Horry County** buyers can actually finance and live in starts long before the home shows up — it starts with the dirt. Here's the honest, plain-English version of what septic, perc tests, and wells really involve, and who handles each piece.

## Why rural Grand Strand lots need this in the first place

Out toward the beach, most lots tie into public sewer and water and you don't think twice about it. But a lot of the affordable, open land around Horry County — the kind families buy to put a new home on — sits where the public lines don't reach. Loris, Longs, Aynor, the rural edges of Conway: plenty of that ground has no sewer at the road and sometimes no water main either.

When that's the case, your home makes its own arrangements. Wastewater goes to a **septic system** buried on your own lot. Drinking water comes from a **well** instead of a public tap. Neither is exotic — it's how much of rural America lives — but both have to be permitted, tested, and built right, and both happen *before* you get keys.

This is also the part of a land deal that's hardest to eyeball. You can judge the trees, the road frontage, and the view. You can't look at a lot and know what the soil will do three feet down. That's what the testing is for.

## The soil evaluation: what a "perc test" actually checks

People say "perc test" — short for percolation, how fast water soaks into the ground — but in South Carolina the real gatekeeper is a **soil evaluation** done for the state. Before anyone approves a septic system on your lot, an evaluator reads the ground itself. Here's roughly what happens:

- **They dig borings.** A minimum of two soil samples are pulled where the septic system would most likely go.
- **They read the color.** Soil color tells them how high the water table climbs in the wettest part of the year. On our flat, low-lying coastal land, that's the number that trips lots up most.
- **They read the texture.** Texture tells them how fast water moves through each layer and how well the soil will filter, or "treat," the wastewater.

That reading decides everything downstream. Good soil means a standard, affordable system. Marginal soil might mean a larger or engineered system that costs more. And once in a while, the soil says a spot won't drain well enough — exactly the kind of thing you want to learn on paper, before you've bought the land.

A few honest realities about soil out here:

- **Wet ground slows the whole thing down.** If a lot is saturated, the evaluation may have to wait for it to dry out. The Grand Strand's flat terrain makes this more common than newcomers expect.
- **Two lots side by side can grade out differently.** The only way to know *yours* is to test *yours*.
- **The system has to match the home.** A four-bedroom plan needs more drainfield than a two-bedroom, so bedroom count, lot size, and soil all have to line up.

## SCDES permits for a septic system manufactured home Horry County buyers can finance

In South Carolina, septic systems are permitted by the state — specifically the **South Carolina Department of Environmental Services (SCDES)**. You'll still hear people say "DHEC" out of habit; septic permitting moved from DHEC to the newly created SCDES in 2024, but it's the same process and the same standards under a new name.

The path is routine once you know it. A septic application (the state's onsite wastewater form) gets filed through the SCDES online permitting portal with a copy of your plat or deed. The soil evaluation gets done. If the site checks out, SCDES issues a **Permit to Construct** — the green light to build the system that fits your home.

Here's the order-of-operations that surprises first-time buyers, and it's the single most important thing on this page: **on a lot without public sewer, Horry County generally won't issue your building permit until SCDES has approved the septic.** Septic isn't a loose end you tidy up at the end — it's a gate near the front of the line, which is why a real soil evaluation is worth its weight in gold before you commit. Our [zoning, setbacks and septic guide](/blog/horry-county-manufactured-home-zoning-setbacks-septic) covers how this fits with the county's side of the rules.

## Well vs. public water

Water follows the same logic as sewer. If there's a public water line at the road, you tap into it and you're done. If there isn't, your lot needs its own **well**.

In South Carolina, residential wells are also overseen by SCDES. A well has to be drilled by a South Carolina certified well driller — not a weekend project — and a notice gets filed with the state first. Once the well is in, it gets **tested for bacteria and contaminants**, and those have to come back clean before the water is cleared for use. That testing is a feature, not red tape: it's how you know the water at your tap is safe to give your kids.

The practical thing to budget for is distance. On a lot that's already been built near, water and power are a short, predictable run. On a deeper parcel, a longer well, power run, or sewer connection is real money — and it's the line item buyers most often forget when they're only looking at the home's price.

## Who actually handles all of this

This is the part where most buyers exhale. You don't have to become an expert in soil borings, SCDES forms, and well drilling to get a finished, financeable home on your land. That coordination is our job, every day, in Horry County.

When we look at a lot with you, we flag early whether the soil and septic look smooth or tricky, whether you're on public water or need a well, and how far the utilities have to travel. Then we coordinate the permitting, the septic or sewer, the well or water tap, and the power — as one package, so the home that arrives is allowed to be there and properly tied in. A clean **septic system manufactured home Horry County** project isn't luck; it's doing these steps in order, with someone who's done it before. You can see how the sequence flows on our [process page](/process), and how it comes together as one deal on our [land-home packages](/land-packages) page. Still shopping for ground? Our guide to [buying land for a manufactured home on the Grand Strand](/blog/buying-land-for-manufactured-home-grand-strand) is a good next read.

The short version: rural land out here is one of the most affordable ways to own a brand-new home — but the septic and the water have to check out first, and the only way to know is to test the specific piece of dirt.

## Let's read your dirt

If you own a lot, or you're eyeing one out around [Conway, Loris, Longs, Aynor, or anywhere along the Grand Strand](/locations), the smartest first move is a real evaluation — not a guess. Send us the address or tax map number and we'll tell you straight what it'll likely take: how it's zoned, where the home can sit, and what septic and water will run.

title: How Much Down Payment Do You Really Need for a Home on Land?
description: Manufactured home down payment requirements explained: FHA ~3.5%, VA & USDA zero down, and how your owned land can cover the down payment in SC.
bodyMarkdown:
If there's one question that stops people cold before they ever call us, it's this one: "How much do I have to have saved up?" The good news is that the manufactured home down payment requirements for a new home on land you own are usually a lot friendlier than folks expect — and if you already own the land, they can get friendlier still.

Here's the honest breakdown of the manufactured home down payment requirements for each loan program, and why buying a new home on owned land changes the math in your favor.

## First, why the loan even works this way

A lot of people grew up thinking of these homes as something you finance with a high-rate, short-term "chattel" loan — the kind you'd use for a car or an RV. That's the old mobile-home world, and it's where the scary down payment myths come from.

A brand-new home from a builder like Clayton, Cavco, or Champion, permanently set on land you own, is a different animal. Once it's affixed to a permanent foundation and titled as **real property** instead of a vehicle, it qualifies for the same mortgage programs as any house: FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional. That single fact — real property, not personal property — is what unlocks the low and no-down options below. (We dig into the real-property side of this in our piece on [real property versus personal property in SC](/blog/manufactured-home-real-property-vs-personal-property-sc).)

## FHA: about 3.5% down

For most first-time buyers around the Grand Strand, FHA is the workhorse. The headline number is **3.5% down** if your credit score is 580 or higher. If your score lands between 500 and 579, you can still qualify on paper, but the down payment steps up to 10% — and in practice many lenders set their own floor higher than FHA's published minimum, so your score still matters.

What does 3.5% mean in plain dollars? On a package priced in the low $200s, you're talking a down payment in the single-digit thousands — not the 20% mountain a lot of people assume they need. FHA also expects the home to be built after June 1976 (every home we sell is brand-new, so that's never an issue) and set on a permanent foundation that meets HUD standards — which is exactly how we place every home.

If you want the deeper FHA walkthrough alongside the VA and conventional options, we laid it all out in [FHA, VA, and conventional financing for manufactured homes in SC](/blog/fha-va-conventional-financing-manufactured-homes-sc).

## VA and USDA: zero down

This is the part people don't believe until they see it written down. Two programs can get you into a new home on land with **no down payment at all**.

- **VA loans.** If you're a qualifying veteran or active-duty service member, the VA allows 100% financing on a home and land together, as long as the home is real property on a permanent foundation. That's zero down on the purchase price. Some lenders ask for a small cushion depending on your profile, but the program itself doesn't require a down payment.
- **USDA Rural Development loans.** Much of Horry and Georgetown County — Loris, Aynor, Longs, the land out past Conway — sits in USDA-eligible rural territory. For buyers under the household income limits, USDA also offers **100% financing, zero down**. New manufactured homes on permanent foundations qualify. Given where so many of our buyers are placing homes, this is a real, common option, not a technicality.

We wrote a whole guide on the USDA route because it surprises so many people: [USDA zero-down manufactured homes in rural Horry County](/blog/usda-zero-down-manufactured-home-rural-horry-county). If you're shopping land out in the county, read it before you assume you need cash.

## Conventional: more down, but it has its place

Conventional loans typically ask for more money up front than FHA — often somewhere in the 5% range or higher depending on the lender and your credit — but they can come with their own advantages, like dropping mortgage insurance sooner once you've built enough equity. For buyers with strong credit and some savings, conventional is worth comparing against FHA rather than assuming one is always better. A good lender will run both side by side so you can see the real monthly difference.

## The part most people miss: your land *is* the down payment

Here's where buying on owned land genuinely changes the conversation. If you already own your lot — inherited family land out toward Aynor, or a parcel you bought a few years back — the equity in that land can count toward your down payment.

In plain terms: lenders following the standard guidelines treat the value of your owned land as your own money toward the deal. If the land is paid off free and clear, that equity can cover **most or all** of what you'd otherwise need to bring in cash. People call this "land-in-lieu" of a down payment, and for families sitting on a piece of ground they already own, it can mean walking into a new home with little or nothing out of pocket.

A few honest caveats so there are no surprises:

- It works best when the land is owned outright with no loans or liens against it.
- If you still owe on the land, a lender can often roll that balance into the new loan and apply your remaining equity — but how much credit you get depends on the appraised value of the land, not what the county has it assessed at.
- Because your land becomes part of the collateral, treat the decision seriously. You're putting real ground behind the loan, and that's exactly why it carries weight with the lender.

If part of your plan is building on a lot the family already has, our guide on [putting a manufactured home on family land](/blog/manufactured-home-on-family-land-conway-aynor) covers how that typically comes together around here.

## The real manufactured home down payment requirements, summed up

The honest answer is: **it depends on the program you qualify for and what you already own.** But to give you a realistic frame:

1. **Veteran or in a USDA-eligible rural area, under income limits?** You may need **zero down**.
2. **Most other buyers?** Plan on roughly **3.5%** with FHA, a bit more with conventional.
3. **Already own your land free and clear?** Your equity may cover the down payment, sometimes entirely.

Closing costs are a separate line from the down payment, and sometimes a seller credit or lender option can help with those too — another thing a real conversation sorts out fast. You can also see how the full package comes together on our [financing page](/financing).

## Let's figure out your actual number

You don't need to guess at this, and you definitely don't need to talk yourself out of a home because of a down payment myth from the mobile-home days. Tell us where you're looking, whether you own land yet, and roughly your situation, and we'll point you to the program that fits — FHA, VA, USDA, conventional, or your own land doing the heavy lifting.

Call Home Placer at **(843) 849-HOME**, and we'll give you a straight answer about what it really takes to get into a new home on land here on the Grand Strand. No pressure — just real numbers for your real situation.

title: Manufactured Home Property Taxes South Carolina: The 4% Rate Explained
description: Manufactured home property taxes South Carolina: how the 4% owner-occupied rate works, why titling on owned land matters, and how to avoid the 6% rate.
bodyMarkdown:
If you're shopping for a new home around the Grand Strand, somebody has probably warned you that "mobile homes" get taxed weird in South Carolina. There's a kernel of truth buried in that — but it's not the whole story, and once you understand how manufactured home property taxes South Carolina charges actually work, it usually lands in your favor, not against you.

Here's the honest version, the part that matters most, and the one thing that quietly decides whether you pay the lower rate or the higher one.

## Two property tax ratios, and why the gap matters

South Carolina taxes most residential property at one of two assessment ratios. That ratio isn't your tax bill — it's the percentage of your home's value the county actually taxes before the local millage gets applied. The two numbers to know:

- **4% — owner-occupied legal residence.** This is the rate for a home you own and live in as your primary, full-time residence.
- **6% — everything else residential.** Second homes, vacation places, rentals, and investment property all fall here.

The structure of the home — stick-built, modular, or manufactured — is not what sets the ratio. What sets it is whether the home is your primary legal residence and whether it's classified as real property in the first place. That second piece is where manufactured homes need a little extra attention, and it's the part dealers don't always explain.

## How a manufactured home becomes "real property"

A brand-new manufactured home doesn't start life as real estate. Out of the factory it has a title, a lot like a vehicle does. If it stays that way — titled as personal property, sitting on land you don't own — it gets treated differently, and you miss out on the cleaner real-property path.

But when you buy a new Clayton, Cavco, or Champion home through a land-home package, set it permanently on **land you own**, and affix it to a foundation, that title gets retired and the home is converted to **real property**. From that point on, the county assesses the home and the land together, the same way it would a site-built house down the road.

We walk through that conversion in detail in our piece on [real property vs. personal property for manufactured homes in SC](/blog/manufactured-home-real-property-vs-personal-property-sc), because it's the hinge the whole tax question swings on. Get the home onto owned land and titled as real property, and you're now playing by the same property-tax rules as any house in Horry or Georgetown County — including eligibility for that 4% legal-residence ratio.

## Manufactured home property taxes South Carolina buyers miss: claiming the 4% rate

Here's the part people miss. Qualifying for the 4% owner-occupied rate is not automatic. The county doesn't read your mind. You have to **apply** for the legal residence classification with the county assessor's office, and you have to do it on time.

In Horry County, that means filing a legal-residence application with the assessor and showing the home is genuinely your primary residence. The documents the county asks for include:

- A **South Carolina driver's license** or state ID showing the property address
- **SC vehicle registration** at that address
- Your **state and federal income tax returns** (or an SSA-1099) showing the property as your home

If you never file, the county defaults you to the **6% ratio** — even though you live there full-time and would clearly qualify. That's the quiet trap. A home that should be taxed at the lower owner-occupied rate gets billed at the higher one simply because nobody filled out the form. The good news: in Horry County you generally only apply once, and the classification stays in place unless your ownership or residency changes. The county has historically asked that applications be in by around the end of May to land on that year's tax bill, so the move is to file soon after you close rather than leave it on the back burner.

To be clear about what we can and can't tell you: we're not going to quote you a dollar figure or a "you'll save X" number, because your actual bill depends on your home's appraised value and the local millage where your lot sits, and those vary. What we can tell you plainly is the rule — primary residence on owned land, titled as real property, filed with the assessor, equals the 4% legal-residence ratio instead of 6%.

## Why buying new on owned land flips the old "mobile home tax" worry

The reputation manufactured homes carry for being taxed strangely mostly comes from the old setup: an older home sitting in a rented park, still on a personal-property title, never converted to real estate. In that world, the home and the land are taxed and titled as two separate things, and none of the clean homeowner advantages apply.

Buying new and placing it on land you own turns that on its head:

- **One parcel, one bill.** Home and land are assessed together as real property, not as a vehicle plus a lot.
- **Access to the 4% ratio.** Because it's now your owner-occupied legal residence, you can apply for the lower assessment ratio like any homeowner.
- **It finances and appraises like a house.** Real property on owned land is what makes the better loan programs possible in the first place — see how that works on our [financing page](/financing).
- **No lot rent feeding someone else's tax bill.** You own the ground. The equity and the tax classification are both yours.

This is the same theme that runs through how these homes [hold their value over time](/blog/do-manufactured-homes-on-permanent-foundations-appreciate) and why an [owned-lot setup beats a leased lot](/blog/owned-land-vs-leased-land-manufactured-home). The manufactured home property taxes South Carolina charges aren't a separate perk — they're part of the same package that comes from doing it the real-property way from day one.

## A simple way to keep it straight

If you only remember a few things about manufactured home property taxes South Carolina applies, make it these:

1. **South Carolina has a 4% owner-occupied rate and a 6% rate** for other residential property.
2. **A new manufactured home on land you own, titled as real property, plays by house rules** — including eligibility for that 4%.
3. **You must apply** with the county assessor to get the 4% rate; skip it and you're billed at 6%.
4. **Don't quote yourself a number off the internet** — your bill depends on appraised value and local millage.

## Let's make sure you're set up the right way

You shouldn't have to guess at any of this. When we place a new home for you on land you own, we'll point you straight at what to file and when so the home is titled as real property and you're positioned for the owner-occupied rate — not stuck on the higher one by accident.

If you're weighing a new manufactured home anywhere from Conway to Loris, Longs, Aynor, or down toward Georgetown, give Home Placer a call at **(843) 849-HOME**. We'll walk the whole picture with you — home, land, financing, and taxes — in plain English, no pressure.

title: New vs. Used Manufactured Home: The Smarter Buy on Land
description: New vs used manufactured home in Horry County, SC: why new wins on warranty, HUD code, USDA financing, and efficiency — and when used still makes sense.
bodyMarkdown:
There's a moment in almost every home search around the Grand Strand where the numbers tempt you toward a used home. A pre-owned manufactured home looks cheaper on the sticker, and cheaper feels safer when you're nervous about a big purchase. But the honest comparison of a new vs used manufactured home is rarely as simple as the price tag makes it look — and on land you own, new usually wins by more than people expect.

We're not going to pretend used never makes sense. Sometimes it does. But you deserve the straight version of the tradeoffs before you sign anything, so here's how we'd lay it out for a neighbor.

## What "used" actually saves you — and what it doesn't

Let's start where the appeal is real. A used manufactured home can cost less up front than a brand-new one. If your whole goal is the lowest possible purchase price today, a used home will usually beat a new one on that single line.

That's the honest pro. Here's the part the sticker doesn't tell you:

- **You're buying its history, not just the home.** Roof age, the condition of the HVAC, plumbing, wiring, how it was set and tied down, whether water ever got in — all of that came with the previous owner, and most of it you can't see on a walk-through.
- **It's sold as-is.** When something fails three months after you move in, that's your bill. There's no one to call.
- **Older means a different rulebook.** A home built before June 15, 1976 isn't a "manufactured home" at all in the eyes of the law — it's a pre-HUD-Code mobile home, and it's genuinely hard to finance, insure, or resell.

So "cheaper" is true on day one. Whether it stays true depends on what you can't see yet.

## New means it's built to today's HUD Code

Every new manufactured home we place — Clayton, Cavco, or Champion — is built to the federal HUD Code, the national construction and safety standard in force since June 15, 1976 and tightened several times since. That code governs structural strength, fire safety, plumbing, electrical, and energy performance, and every home gets a red certification label proving it passed.

The "tightened several times since" part matters more than it sounds in a new vs used manufactured home decision. An older home was built to an older version of the code — or, if it predates 1976, to no national standard at all. A home placed today is built to the current one. Here on the coast, that also means it's built for the right **wind zone** for Horry and Georgetown counties — Wind Zone II, the coastal-strength standard — which is not something you want to guess about when you live an hour from the Atlantic. With a used home, you inherit whatever wind standard, if any, was in force when it was first built.

## The warranty gap is the biggest difference

This is the one that should move the needle most, and it's simple.

A new home from Home Placer comes backed by real, written coverage: a full **one-year home warranty** on the home itself, plus a **2-10 Home Buyers Warranty** — that's two years on the systems (plumbing, electrical, HVAC) and ten years on the major structural bones — and a **30-day walk-through** after you've lived in it for a month. If something's off, you have a number to call and a team that answers. We walk through exactly how that works in [our breakdown of what's covered](/warranty).

A used home almost never comes with any of that. The factory warranty expired with the first owner. You're buying it as-is, and every repair is yours. For a lot of buyers, that's the entire difference between a calm first year and a stressful one.

## Financing often favors new — especially USDA

Here's a piece that genuinely surprises people: the loan you qualify for can depend on whether the home is new or used.

A lot of rural Horry County — the stretches out toward Conway, Loris, Longs, and Aynor — falls inside USDA-eligible territory, and a USDA Rural Development loan can mean **$0 down**. But USDA leans heavily toward new construction: for a manufactured home, the unit generally has to be **new**, transported straight from the manufacturer to your site and never previously installed or occupied somewhere else. In plain terms, you usually **cannot** use a USDA loan to buy a typical used manufactured home. So for a buyer counting on $0 down, choosing used can quietly close the door on the very program that made the home affordable.

New also keeps your other roads open. A new home permanently set on land you own, titled as real property, can qualify for FHA (as little as 3.5% down), VA (often $0 down for eligible veterans), and conventional financing. Older homes — especially anything pre-1976 — tend to get pushed toward chattel (personal-property) loans with shorter terms and higher rates, the kind people wrongly assume is the *only* way to finance a manufactured home. It isn't, when the home is new and on your land. We lay the loan types out side by side in our [guide to FHA, VA, and conventional financing](/blog/fha-va-conventional-financing-manufactured-homes-sc).

## Energy efficiency you actually feel on the power bill

The HUD Code's energy requirements have climbed over the decades. Older homes were built with thinner insulation and less air-sealing than today's standards call for; a new home is built to current energy rules, with better insulation, tighter ducts, and modern windows.

You don't see that on a sticker, but you feel it every July when the Grand Strand humidity rolls in and your HVAC is running hard. A more efficient home costs less to keep comfortable, month after month, and that ongoing savings is real money a lower used-home price can quietly eat back up.

## When used might still make sense

We promised honest, so here it is. Used can be the right call if:

- You're paying **cash** and the up-front number is the only thing that matters to you.
- You've had a **thorough, independent inspection** and you go in clear-eyed about repairs.
- It's a **post-1976 home in genuinely good shape**, and you're not relying on USDA or a long-term low-rate mortgage to make it work.

If that's you, a used home can be a reasonable buy. Just go in knowing you're trading the warranty, the newest code, the efficiency, and some financing doors for a lower price.

## The bottom line on a new vs used manufactured home

For most buyers we meet — financing the purchase, planning to stay a while, and putting the home on land they own — new is the smarter buy. You get current HUD-Code construction, the full warranty package, the widest financing options including USDA's $0-down path, and a home that's cheaper to run. And because it's permanently set on land you own, it behaves like real estate, not a depreciating box on a rented lot — which is exactly why [a new home on a permanent foundation can hold and build value over time](/blog/do-manufactured-homes-on-permanent-foundations-appreciate).

If you want to walk a few new floor plans and see how the numbers compare for your situation, take a look at [the homes we carry](/homes) or just give us a call. We'll lay out new and used honestly, point you toward the financing that fits, and never push you toward a number we can't stand behind. title: How Long Do Manufactured Homes Last? An Honest Answer
description: How long do manufactured homes last? A new, HUD-code home on a permanent foundation can last decades. Honest answer for Grand Strand buyers.
bodyMarkdown:
It's one of the first questions people ask when they start looking at a brand-new manufactured home: how long do manufactured homes last? It's a fair question, and you deserve a straight answer instead of a sales pitch. So here it is, plainly, the way we'd explain it to a neighbor over the fence.

The honest version is this: a new, quality-built manufactured home that's set up right and looked after can last for decades, every bit as long as you'd expect a home you raise a family in to last. The catch is in those two phrases, "set up right" and "looked after." Get those wrong, and you shorten the life of any home. Get them right, and you've got a place that holds up for the long haul.

## So How Long Do Manufactured Homes Last?

You'll see a lot of numbers thrown around online, and they range widely because they're lumping together everything from a 1972 trailer to a brand-new HUD-code home. That's not a fair comparison, and it's the main reason the answer to "how long do manufactured homes last" feels so muddy.

Here's the cleaner way to think about it. The lifespan of a manufactured home isn't one fixed number stamped on it at the factory. It's the result of three things working together:

- **How it was built** — older mobile homes and today's HUD-code homes are not the same animal.
- **How it was set up** — a permanent foundation versus a quick, temporary set changes everything.
- **How it's maintained** — the same care that protects any house protects this one.

Nail all three and you're looking at a home that serves you for many decades. That's not wishful thinking; it's just how durable construction, a solid foundation, and basic upkeep add up.

## The 1976 Line: Why the Old Reputation Doesn't Apply

A big part of the "they don't last" reputation comes from homes built before there were real rules. That changed in **1976**. Since June 15 of that year, every manufactured home built in this country has had to meet the federal HUD Code, a national construction and safety standard that didn't exist before.

Before the HUD Code, "mobile homes" were built to all kinds of standards, or none at all. Quality was a coin flip. After 1976, the rules got specific and they've been tightened several times since. Today's HUD-code homes from builders like **Clayton, Cavco, and Champion** are engineered for structural strength, fire safety, energy efficiency, and wind resistance. You can read more about how those three [home brands compare](/brands) if you're weighing them.

Here's the part that matters for lifespan: a pre-1976 trailer and a new HUD-code home aren't in the same conversation. When somebody tells you "those homes only last 15 or 20 years," they're usually describing a home built before the standards existed, in an era when nobody was inspecting the work. That's not what you're buying when you buy new.

## Why a Permanent Foundation Is the Whole Ballgame

If there's one factor that decides how long your home lasts, it's how it sits on the ground.

A home that's set on a temporary support system, with no permanent foundation and no tie to the land, is more exposed to moisture, shifting, and the slow wear that comes from not being properly anchored. A home set on a **permanent foundation** is a different story. The foundation is built of durable materials, concrete or masonry, and designed to last the life of the home. It anchors the structure, keeps it level, and protects it from the ground up.

There's a financial side to this too. When your new home is permanently affixed to land you own, it's titled as **real property**, the same legal category as any site-built house. That's what makes it financeable with conventional, FHA, VA, or USDA loans, and it's a big reason these homes [hold their value over time](/blog/do-manufactured-homes-hold-value). A home that's planted, not parked, behaves like real estate, because that's exactly what it is.

This is the whole idea behind how we do things at Home Placer: a brand-new home, set on a permanent foundation, on land you own, as one package. We're not dropping a box on a rented lot. We're building you a home that's meant to stay put and last.

## Maintenance: The Part That's Actually in Your Hands

Construction and foundation get you to the starting line. Maintenance is what carries the home the rest of the way, and the good news is none of it is complicated or expensive. It's the same short list of habits that protect any home:

- **Watch the roof.** Inspect it once a year and after big storms. Catch a small leak before it becomes a ceiling.
- **Manage moisture.** Keep gutters clear, make sure water drains away from the home, and check that skirting and vents are doing their job. Trapped moisture is the slow enemy of any house.
- **Keep it level.** A permanent foundation does most of this work, but it's worth checking that everything stays sound over the years.
- **Keep up the systems.** Service the HVAC, keep an eye on plumbing and electrical, and replace worn parts before they fail. These are the same systems any home has.
- **Reseal and refresh.** Caulk around windows and doors, touch up exterior finishes, and handle the small stuff before it turns into the big stuff.

Do these things and you protect both the lifespan of the home and its value. Skip them, and you'd shorten the life of a brick house just the same. The home will go the distance; it just needs an owner who shows up for the easy stuff.

## A Straight Answer on the Tradeoffs

We try to be honest about everything here, so we'll say it plainly: a manufactured home, like any home, can be neglected into an early grave. If it's set on a temporary foundation, left to take on moisture, and never maintained, it won't last what it could. That's true of any structure, but it's worth naming.

The flip side is the part most people never hear. Buy **new**, set it on a **permanent foundation**, place it on **land you own**, and keep up with basic maintenance, and you've removed nearly every reason these homes ever earned a short-lifespan reputation. You're left with a well-built, modern home that's covered by a [real warranty](/warranty) out of the gate and built to be lived in for the long term. If you're early in the process, our [step-by-step process](/process) walks through exactly how a home gets from the factory to a permanent foundation on your land.

So, how long do manufactured homes last? When you do it right, long enough to raise a family, pay off a loan, and pass something real on. That's the honest answer, and it's a good one.

title: Can You Actually Build Equity in a Manufactured Home?
description: Can you build equity in a manufactured home? Yes — on land you own, with a real mortgage and appreciation. Here is how it works in coastal SC.
bodyMarkdown:
"Everybody knows a manufactured home is just a depreciating box — you'll never build a dime of equity in one." If you've heard that and it stopped you cold, good. So let's answer it straight: can you actually **build equity in a manufactured home**, or are you throwing money at something that only loses value?

The honest answer is yes — but only one way of buying does it. The difference between the way that builds equity and the way that doesn't is the single most important thing on this page.

## What "equity" actually means

Equity isn't a feeling or a sales pitch. It's a number: what your property is worth minus what you still owe on it. Two forces grow that number over time, and a home has to be set up to catch both.

- **Paying down a real mortgage.** Every month, part of your payment chips away at the loan balance (the principal). As that balance drops, the slice you own outright gets bigger. It's forced savings, built into your payment.
- **The property going up in value (appreciation).** In real estate, the land is usually what appreciates, not the structure. When your home is tied to land you own, it can ride the local market up the same way any house does. (We dig into when that actually happens in our piece on [whether homes on permanent foundations appreciate](/blog/do-manufactured-homes-on-permanent-foundations-appreciate).)

Rent does neither of those things. Lot rent in a park does neither. To **build equity in a manufactured home**, you need a setup that lets both forces work for you — a real loan you're paying down, and real land underneath that can gain value.

## Why owned land is the whole ballgame

Here's the fork in the road, and almost everything else traces back to it. When you buy a manufactured home, the home and the dirt under it can be tied together two completely different ways.

**Leased land (a park).** You rent the lot and pay lot rent every month, usually with yearly increases. The home stays titled as personal property — the same legal category as a car or a boat — and it's typically financed with a chattel loan. Lot rent builds you nothing, and a vehicle-titled home on rented dirt behaves like the depreciating asset its title says it is.

**Owned land.** You own the home and the land as one piece of real estate. The home sits on a permanent foundation, the old vehicle title is retired, and the whole thing becomes real property — the same legal category as any traditional house. No lot rent. No landlord. A real mortgage you're paying down, on land that can appreciate.

That second path is the only one we do at Home Placer. We've never put a family on leased land, and we never will — because that's exactly the setup that can't build equity. We go deeper on this fork in our piece on [owned land vs. leased land](/blog/owned-land-vs-leased-land-manufactured-home), but the short version: owning the dirt is what turns a "mobile home" into a real home with real equity.

## How you build equity in a manufactured home

Here's the actual machine that builds equity on an owned-land package:

1. **You own land** (or buy it as part of the package), and we set a brand-new Clayton, Cavco, or Champion home on a permanent foundation.
2. **The title gets retired** and the home converts to real property — home and land become one parcel of real estate.
3. **You finance it with a real mortgage** instead of a higher-rate chattel loan, so every payment pays down principal you own.
4. **The property tracks the local market**, which around here stays in demand.

Each step is a piece of equity the leased-land buyer never gets. Step three is the one people underestimate, so let's slow down on it.

## Real property unlocks real mortgages — and real mortgages build equity

A home titled as personal property on a rented lot is usually stuck with a chattel loan: shorter term, higher rate, the kind you'd get on an RV. Convert that same home to real property on land you own, and you unlock the full menu of mortgages a stick-built house gets — **FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional**. That's not just a better rate; it's the engine of your equity:

- **FHA** lets qualified buyers in with as little as **3.5% down**.
- **VA** (for eligible veterans) and **USDA** (in rural-designated areas, and a lot of Horry County qualifies) can go all the way to **zero down**.
- All of them require basically the same thing — a permanent foundation, real-property classification, and that you own the land underneath.

Every one of those is a long-term, amortizing loan — a fancy way of saying every single payment buys you a little more of your own home. Lenders don't write 30-year, government-backed mortgages on depreciating assets; the fact that these homes qualify tells you how the market really categorizes them. We lay out which loan fits which buyer on our [financing page](/financing).

## "But don't manufactured homes always lose value?"

This is the honest objection, so here's the honest answer. The "they always lose value" reputation is earned — but by a specific kind of home: older homes, on rented lots, with a vehicle title and no land attached. Strip the land out of any home and what's left behaves like a depreciating asset. That's the leased-land scenario, and it's real.

But every manufactured home built today is constructed to the federal HUD Code, the national building standard in force since **June 15, 1976** and strengthened several times since. And here on the coast it matters that Horry and Georgetown counties sit in **HUD Wind Zone II** — the stricter coastal tier, built to stand up to 100-mph winds — so new homes delivered here are engineered for tougher wind loads than homes built for inland (Zone I) areas. Put a solid, code-built home on land you own, and you've assembled the two ingredients that actually drive value: a real structure and appreciating ground beneath it. We get deeper into this in our piece on [whether manufactured homes hold their value](/blog/do-manufactured-homes-hold-value) — but the short of it is the myth describes the rented lot, not what we build.

## The tax angle that quietly helps

One more piece most buyers never hear about. In South Carolina, an owner-occupied legal residence — including a manufactured home you own and live in on your own land — is assessed at the **4% ratio**, the same favorable rate as any primary home, while many other setups fall into the higher **6%** bracket. Lower carrying costs over the years leave more room for the equity to do its work.

## This is a real, active market — not a theory

You don't have to take any of this on faith. Over the past several months we've placed brand-new homes on owned land across Conway, Loris, Longs, Aynor, and the Myrtle Beach area — real lots, real buyers, recorded as real property. We won't put made-up return percentages in front of you, but a steady stream of new homes closing as real estate is the clearest sign there is that buyers and lenders treat these as the real deal. You can browse the actual homes we've set on our [recently placed](/recently-placed) page.

## The bottom line

A used home on a rented lot is a tough place to build equity — that part of the reputation is fair. A brand-new home on a permanent foundation, on land you own, titled as real property and financed with a real mortgage, is a different animal. It builds equity the same two ways every other house on the street does: you pay down the loan, and the land can appreciate.

If you've got a lot in mind, or you're just trying to figure out whether the numbers work for your situation, that's the conversation we have every day here in Horry County. Call Home Placer at **(843) 849-HOME** and we'll walk through the real math with you — no hype, no pressure.

title: Energy-Efficient New Manufactured Homes: Lower Bills by Design
description: Energy efficient manufactured homes use modern HUD/DOE standards, insulation, windows and HVAC to cut bills below an old mobile home on the Grand Strand.
bodyMarkdown:
If your only picture of a "trailer" is a drafty single-wide from the 1980s with a window unit fighting a losing battle against a July afternoon, it's fair to expect a scary power bill. But that picture is decades out of date. Today's energy efficient manufactured homes are built to federal standards an old mobile home never had to meet — and on the Grand Strand, where the AC runs hard from spring to fall, that difference shows up every month on your bill.

Let's walk through what actually makes a new home efficient, in plain terms, without the green-marketing fog.

## Why an old mobile home and a new home aren't the same animal

This is the part people miss, and it changes everything.

Before June 15, 1976, factory-built homes were just "mobile homes," built to whatever rules a given state or factory felt like following. Insulation was thin, windows were single-pane, and there was no national standard holding anyone to a number. That's the home most people picture when they imagine high energy costs — and they're not wrong about *that* home.

On June 15, 1976, HUD — the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development — put a single national construction and safety code in place. Everything built to it since is a **manufactured home**, and from the start that code included energy requirements: minimum insulation, a sealed thermal envelope, and heating equipment sized to actually hold the house at a comfortable temperature. Every home carries a data plate — usually inside a kitchen cabinet or near the electrical panel — that lists the thermal zone it was built for, so the insulation level isn't a sales claim, it's printed on the home.

So when you compare a new home to a 1985 mobile home, you're not comparing two versions of the same thing. You're comparing a home built to a real energy standard against one built to almost none.

## What makes energy efficient manufactured homes efficient

Efficiency isn't one feature. It's a handful of things working together, and a new home from a builder like Clayton, Cavco, or Champion is engineered around all of them.

- **Insulation, in the floor, walls, and ceiling.** The whole point of the thermal envelope is to slow heat from sneaking in during summer and out in winter. The HUD Code sets a minimum for the home's thermal zone, and South Carolina sits in the warmest zone, where the priority is keeping the cooling load down. More insulation means the AC cycles less to hold the same temperature.
- **Better windows.** New homes come with modern double-pane, often low-E windows that reflect heat instead of letting it pour in. That's a world apart from the single-pane glass on an older home.
- **A properly sized, modern HVAC system.** A new home is paired with current-generation heating and cooling equipment, sized to the house. An oversized or worn-out unit is one of the biggest hidden energy hogs in an old home.
- **A tighter, better-sealed shell.** Built indoors on a line, a new home gets its seams, joints, and ductwork sealed in a controlled setting. Less air leaking means less conditioned air you paid for escaping into the yard.

None of this is exotic. It's just what "built to today's code" quietly buys you that an old home never had.

## The standards keep getting stricter

Here's something worth knowing, because it tells you which direction this is all moving.

In 2022 the U.S. Department of Energy finalized new energy conservation standards for manufactured housing, built on the 2021 International Energy Conservation Code — the same modern efficiency benchmark used for site-built homes. Those standards raise the bar on insulation, windows, and air-sealing. We won't pretend to recite every compliance date, because the federal timeline has been pushed back more than once. The takeaway that matters for you is simpler: the floor for what counts as efficient in a new manufactured home is rising, not falling. A home built now is held to a tougher standard than one built ten years ago.

If you want the next level up, there's a voluntary path too. The EPA's **ENERGY STAR** program certifies manufactured homes that are independently verified to beat the baseline — extra sealing, higher-performing components, third-party inspection. Not every home is certified, and we won't promise you a specific badge on a specific floor plan, but if low bills are your top priority, it's a real option worth asking about. You can see the builders and lines we carry on our [brands page](/brands), and we'll tell you straight which ones offer efficiency upgrades.

## Why "new on owned land" stretches the savings further

There's a money angle here that goes beyond the power bill.

Because we set these homes on a permanent foundation on land you own, they're titled as **real property** — a house, not a vehicle on a rented lot. That status is what lets a new home qualify for conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA financing instead of the higher-rate loans tied to older mobile homes. A lower interest rate and an efficient home pulling down your utility costs work in the same direction: a more comfortable total monthly cost of living in the house, not just the sticker. We dig into how that real-property status works in our post on [why a permanent foundation changes everything](/blog/manufactured-home-real-property-vs-personal-property-sc), and we break down the loan options in our guide to [FHA, VA, and conventional financing](/blog/fha-va-conventional-financing-manufactured-homes-sc).

It also means the efficiency was built to stay. Permanent foundation, sealed and insulated to code, real utility hookups — not a temporary setup somebody might cut corners on.

## What we'll tell you straight

We're not going to hand you a dollar figure for your future power bill. Nobody honest can, because it depends on your floor plan, your thermostat habits, how shaded your lot is, and a Grand Strand summer that does what it wants. Anyone quoting you exact "savings" off a brochure is guessing.

What we *can* say plainly: a new home is built to a real, current energy standard, and that standard keeps tightening. The insulation, the windows, the sealed shell, and a right-sized HVAC are all engineered in from the factory — and an old mobile home simply never had to meet any of it. If your goal is to stop pouring money out the windows, starting with new construction is the honest head start.

## See what's possible

The fear of a runaway power bill almost always traces back to picturing the wrong home — an old, leaky one. A new, well-insulated home built to current standards and set right on your land is a different story, and a different bill.

Take a look at the [homes we place around the Grand Strand](/homes), or if you're still weighing builders, our honest breakdown of [Clayton, Cavco, and Champion](/blog/clayton-cavco-champion-brand-comparison) is a good next read. When you're ready for the straight version for your lot and your budget, call Home Placer at **(843) 849-HOME**. We'll walk you through how your home would be built, insulated, and set — no hype, just the honest picture.

We've set new homes on land all over Longs — there's a cluster of them on Pint Circle, from an efficient three-bedroom single-wide on a quarter-acre to a four-bedroom double-wide on a half-acre-plus lot. ## The honest tradeoffs

We'd be doing you no favors if we only sold you the upside. Going inland to Loris or Longs means:

title: The Questions to Ask Before You Buy a Manufactured Home (Buyer Checklist)
description: Owned or leased land? Real property? Permanent foundation? The questions to ask before buying a manufactured home in coastal SC.
bodyMarkdown:
Buying a brand-new home is one of the biggest decisions most people ever make, and the smartest buyers aren't the ones who know everything — they're the ones who ask the right questions before they sign. The questions to ask before buying a manufactured home aren't complicated, but the answers decide whether you end up with a real asset on your own ground or a payment on something that quietly loses value.

So here's the checklist we'd hand a nervous first-time buyer around the Grand Strand. These are the questions to ask before buying a manufactured home, seven of them, each with why it matters. Ask them of anyone trying to sell you a home and you'll already be ahead of most buyers.

## 1. Is the home going on land I own, or land I lease?

This is the first question to ask before buying a manufactured home, because everything hangs on it.

If you lease the lot — a park or "land-lease" community — you own the home but rent the dirt under it. The rent can go up, the park can sell, and a home on a rented lot is hard to resell and rarely worth what you paid. If you own the land, the home and ground are one piece of real estate, with no lot rent and no landlord.

**Why it matters:** owned land is the foundation for real-property titling, real mortgages, and a home that can actually appreciate. We only ever do owned-land packages, and we explain the full fork in the road in [owned land vs. leased land](/blog/owned-land-vs-leased-land-manufactured-home).

## 2. Will the home be titled as personal property or real property?

Here's a term worth knowing: a new manufactured home usually starts life with a **vehicle-style title** — the same legal category as a car or boat. That's "personal property," and left that way it behaves like a depreciating asset and only qualifies for higher-rate loans.

When the home is permanently affixed to land you own, that vehicle title gets retired and the home becomes **real property** — the same legal category as any house.

**Why it matters:** real-property titling is what unlocks the better financing and the better tax treatment. In South Carolina, a home you own and live in as your primary residence is assessed at the state's lower owner-occupied legal-residence ratio instead of the higher rate on second homes and rentals — but only once it's titled as real estate and claimed with the county. We walk through the whole title question in [personal property vs. real property](/blog/manufactured-home-real-property-vs-personal-property-sc).

## 3. Will it be set on a permanent foundation?

Some sellers will quietly set a home on a temporary or minimal setup to shave a little off the price. It feels like a smart cut. It isn't.

A permanent foundation is what turns the home from personal property into real property in the eyes of the county and your lender. No permanent foundation, no real-property title — and without that title, the good loans simply aren't on the table.

**Why it matters:** FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional financing all require the home to sit on a permanent foundation and be taxed as real estate. Treat the foundation as non-negotiable. In a package, it's already baked in.

## 4. What financing will I actually qualify for — and what's the total monthly?

Don't let anyone show you a home price and call it a payment. The two numbers that matter are the **loan type** and the **all-in monthly cost**.

A home on leased land with a vehicle title usually means a **chattel loan** — higher interest, shorter term, fewer protections. A home on owned land, on a permanent foundation and titled as real property, can usually be financed like any other house: FHA at 3.5% down, VA and USDA at zero down for those who qualify, or conventional.

**Why it matters:** same buyer, same home, very different payment. And the real monthly number isn't just principal and interest — it's principal, interest, **property taxes, and insurance** together. Ask for that all-in figure before you fall in love with a floor plan. We break the loan types down on our [financing](/financing) page.

## 5. Is the home built and rated for our wind zone?

We live on the coast, and that matters more than people realize. Every manufactured home is built to the federal HUD Code, and that standard gets tougher near the ocean. Horry and Georgetown counties sit in **HUD Wind Zone II**, the coastal tier built to withstand higher winds than homes headed inland.

The wind rating is printed on the home's **data plate** — usually in a closet, near the breaker panel, or inside a cabinet — and the county permit office checks it during installation.

**Why it matters:** buy a home rated for the wrong zone and the county won't approve the setup, and you can't permit your way around it after the fact. Make sure the home is rated for our area and set by people who do it here every day. More in [will a manufactured home survive a hurricane](/blog/manufactured-home-hurricane-wind-zone-2-sc).

## 6. What warranty comes with it — and is the home new or used?

A used home can look like a bargain, and sometimes it is. But buying used often means inheriting someone else's wiring, someone else's roof, and **no warranty** when something breaks. Older units can also predate the modern HUD code, limiting financing and insurance.

Federal law requires at least a one-year manufacturer warranty on a new home. Builders like Clayton, Cavco, and Champion cover defects in materials and workmanship — structure, plumbing, electrical, and heating — for the first year after install, with longer coverage available on many homes.

**Why it matters:** with a new home, if something's off in that first year it gets handled instead of becoming your problem. Always price a new home before settling for used.

## 7. Is the land actually ready — and is the whole thing one quote?

A home price is not a move-in price. The land underneath has to be **ready**: graded, with a well or water tap, septic or sewer, power, and a proper pad. Skip that planning and surprise costs pile up fast.

**Why it matters:** the only number that means anything is the all-in, on-the-land, ready-to-live-in figure. Ask whether the home, land, delivery, foundation, and site work all live in **one quote and one closing** — or whether you're handed a box and left to sort out the rest. Our [process](/process) page walks through how a real placement goes, start to finish.

## The short version: the questions to ask before buying a manufactured home

Most of these questions rhyme with each other. They come down to one idea: treat the home like the real, permanent thing it can be, not a temporary one.

Own the land. Get the real-property title. Set it on a permanent foundation. Finance it like a house. Match the wind zone. Buy new with a warranty. Price the whole site, not just the box. Get those right and you don't have a "mobile home" — you have a new home, on your own ground, with a payment that can land near or below what you'd pay to rent. For the wrong turns to avoid, we list them in [the biggest mistakes buying a manufactured home](/blog/biggest-mistakes-buying-a-manufactured-home).

## Let's talk it through

You don't have to memorize all of this, and you definitely shouldn't learn it the hard way. If you're early in your research, bring your questions — there's no wrong one. Call Home Placer at **(843) 849-HOME**, tell us roughly where you'd like to be, and we'll give you a real, all-in number for a new home on land you own. Straight answers, no pressure.

title: Move-In Ready Manufactured Home vs. Build-to-Order: Which Fits?
description: Move in ready manufactured home or build-to-order on the Grand Strand? Honest tradeoffs on timeline, customization, and certainty to help you decide.
bodyMarkdown:
When you start shopping for a new home around the Grand Strand, you hit a fork in the road fast: do you take a move in ready manufactured home that's already built and placed, or order a model from the factory and customize it to your taste? Both are good answers. They're just good for different people.

Here's the honest breakdown of each path — what you trade, what you gain, and how to tell which one fits you — so you can decide with your eyes open instead of guessing.

## The two paths, in plain English

There's no wrong door here. It comes down to what you value more: speed and certainty, or choice and customization.

- **Move-in ready** — a brand-new home that's already on a lot, finished, and waiting. You see the actual home, on the actual land, before you buy. What you walk through is what you get.
- **Build-to-order** — you pick a floor plan from a builder like Clayton, Cavco, or Champion, choose your finishes, and we have it built and set on a lot. You're designing it; you just have to wait for it to be built.

To be clear, both are brand-new HUD Code homes — built in a factory to the federal construction standard that's been in place since June 15, 1976 and inspected during production. The difference is timing and choice, not quality.

## When a move in ready manufactured home makes sense

A move in ready manufactured home is the right call more often than people expect. Here's who it fits.

- **You need to be in soon.** If your lease is ending, you sold your old place, or you're just tired of waiting, a finished home skips the build queue. The big time cost — manufacturing and site work — is already behind it.
- **You want to see it before you commit.** Some folks have a hard time picturing a home from a floor plan and a finish board. With a ready home, you walk the rooms, stand in the kitchen, and feel the space. No imagination required.
- **You like certainty on the number.** When the home is built and placed, the surprises are mostly out of the system. The lot is graded, the well or tap and septic or sewer are in, the power's run. You're buying a known quantity, not a forecast.
- **You're financing and want a clean path.** A finished home on land you own is real property, which keeps your loan options open — FHA, VA, USDA, or conventional instead of the higher-rate loans tied to homes in rented parks.

The tradeoff is honest: with a ready home, you take it largely as it is. The floor plan is set, the finishes are chosen, the lot is the lot. If one is already close to what you wanted, that's a feature, not a compromise. You can see what we've recently finished and placed on our [recently placed homes](/recently-placed) page — those are real examples of the ready path.

## When build-to-order is the better fit

Ordering a model is the right move when the home itself, or the land, has to be a specific way.

- **You have a clear picture in your head.** You want a particular floor plan, a certain number of bedrooms, a kitchen laid out your way. Build-to-order lets you choose the plan and the finishes instead of settling for what's already standing.
- **You already own the land — or a specific lot.** If the home is going on [family land](/blog/manufactured-home-on-family-land-conway-aynor) or a lot you've already picked out, build-to-order is built around that. You're matching the home to the ground, not the other way around.
- **You want to compare brands and plans.** This is the path where you really shop. Browse the models, weigh the [differences between Clayton, Cavco, and Champion](/blog/clayton-cavco-champion-brand-comparison), and pick the plan that earns its keep. Start on our [homes](/homes) page to order a model.

The tradeoff here is time and patience. A custom home has to be built and then delivered, set, and connected. It's worth the wait when the result is exactly what you wanted — but it is a wait, and you're committing before you can walk the finished rooms. If you want a realistic sense of the schedule, our breakdown of the [home-on-land timeline in Horry County](/blog/manufactured-home-on-land-timeline-horry-county) lays out the steps honestly.

## Timeline: the real difference

This is where the two paths split most clearly.

A **move in ready manufactured home** is, by definition, ready. Once you're approved and the paperwork moves, you're looking at a closing timeline rather than a construction timeline. The slow parts — the factory build, the grading, the utility hookups — are already done.

**Build-to-order** runs longer because you're starting the clock at the factory. The home has to be manufactured, then trucked to your lot, set, anchored, and connected to water, septic or sewer, and power. None of that is unusual, and we coordinate all of it — but it's weeks of work that a ready home has already finished.

Neither timeline is "better." A ready home wins on speed. A build-to-order home wins on getting precisely what you pictured. The question is which one you'd rather spend.

## Customization: how much do you actually want?

Be honest with yourself here, because it's the question that usually settles the whole decision.

If you've got a strong vision — a specific plan, finishes you care about, a layout in your head — build-to-order is built for you, and a ready home will probably feel like a compromise. But plenty of buyers don't have a rigid picture. They want a solid, new three- or four-bedroom home, on land they own, at a payment that works. For them, a finished home that's already most of the way to what they wanted is the smarter buy, because they get all the speed and certainty without giving up much.

There's no prize for customizing more than you care to. The best path is the one that matches how particular you actually are — not how particular you think you're supposed to be.

## A simple way to decide

Run yourself through these quick gut-checks:

1. **How soon do you need to move?** Sooner pushes you toward move-in ready.
2. **Do you have a specific floor plan or finishes in mind?** A strong yes pushes you toward build-to-order.
3. **Is there a particular lot or piece of land driving the decision?** That usually points to build-to-order, built around the land.
4. **Would you rather see the exact home first, or design it first?** That single preference tells you most of what you need to know.

There's no wrong answer. There's just the answer that fits your life right now. And honestly, the fastest way to know is to look at both — walk a ready home, then look at the models you'd order — and see which one feels right.

You don't have to settle this on paper. Come see what's actually [recently placed and ready](/recently-placed), browse the [models you can order](/homes), and if you want to understand exactly how a build comes together from contract to keys, walk through our [process](/process) page.

Either path ends the same good way: a brand-new home on land you own, no lot rent, no HOA. Call Home Placer at **(843) 849-HOME**, tell us roughly when you'd like to be in and how particular you are about the details, and we'll point you to the path that fits.
